title: UPDATE 1- Currency intervention  costly and inefficient,  Norway  c.bank chief says
text:
(Updates with comment on currency intervention, quote)

OSLO, May 9 (Reuters) -

Currency market intervention is costly and unlikely to be an efficient policy tool over time, Norway's central bank Governor Ida Wolden Bache told a hearing in parliament on Tuesday.

"Historical experience... shows that currency interventions to secure a certain level of the currency are costly and not very efficient over time," Bache said.

Norway's floating currency exchange rate allows the country to set policy interest rates at levels that are the most appropriate for the economic outlook, she said.

Norges Bank

last intervened

in the currency market to support the crown in March 2020 to counter a slump during the early stage of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Bache reiterated that Norges Bank's currency transactions on behalf of the government and the sovereign wealth fund are not part of the country's monetary policy. (Reporting by Terje Solsvik, editing by Anna Ringstrom)

title: FOREX -Yen rallies after Japan  intervenes  with first support since 1998
text:
* 
      "We have taken decisive action," says Japan's Kanda 
    

        * 
      Dollar still up 23% despite Japan intervention
    

        * 
      Sterling, Swiss franc, Norway's crown slide after rate hikes 
    

        * 
      Dollar hits new multi-year high vs sterling, euro
    

  
 (New throughout, updates prices, market activity and comments)
    By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss and Alun John
       NEW YORK/LONDON, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The Japanese yen soared across the board on Thursday after
monetary authorities intervened in the foreign exchange market to boost the battered currency for the first
time since 1998, although analysts said Japan may struggle to keep the yen strong.
    The dollar was last down 1.2% at 142.33 yen. It hit a low of 140.31 after the intervention,
having earlier reached a fresh 24-year peak of 145.9 yen. The spread between the day's high and low for the
pair was the widest since June 2016. 
    North American traders cautiously pushed the dollar higher against the yen after Japan stepped in, but
for now, few are challenging Japan's action.
        "The market is nervous," said Steven Englander, head of global G10 FX research and North America
macro strategy at Standard Chartered in New York. 
  
        "There is a risk that Japan becomes a permanent presence in the market for intervention to be
successful. Not that Japan has to step in everyday, but the market has to be afraid of intervention," he
added.
  
    The euro, pound, Swiss franc, the Australian and New Zealand dollars, among others, also plunged against
the yen. 
    "We have taken decisive action," Japan's Vice Finance Minister for international affairs Masato Kanda
told reporters, responding in the affirmative when asked if that meant intervention.
    Confirmation of the intervention came just hours after the BOJ decided to maintain low interest rates to
support the country's fragile economic recovery.
    BOJ Governor Haruhiko Kuroda told reporters the central bank could hold off on hiking rates or changing
its dovish policy guidance for years.
    In contrast, central banks around the world, most notably the Federal Reserve, are raising rates
aggressively and the policy divergence has weighed on the yen. 
    However, analysts said Japan can't keep propping up the currency on a sustained basis.
    "Over the next three to six months or possibly even longer, as long as those diverging paths of monetary
policy are still in place and those differences persist, you'll continue to see a weaker yen," said Brendan
McKenna, international economist and FX Strategist at Wells Fargo Securities. 
    Even after Thursday's moves, the dollar is still up 23.6% against the yen so far this year, on track for
its largest yearly percentage gain in 43 years.
    CENTRAL BANK BONANZA 
    In a busy day for markets, the pound pared the small advance it had made in London trading after the
Bank of England raised interest rates by 50 basis points. 
    The hike was in line with expectations, although markets had been pricing in a small chance of a larger
75 bp move. 
    Sterling was last down 0.2% at $1.1251, not too far from a fresh 37-year low of $1.1213, hit in
Asia trading. 
    The euro was little changed at $0.9832, recovering from a new 20-year trough of $0.9807 hit
earlier in the global session.
    The dollar index, which measures the greenback's value against a basket of six  major currencies,
slipped 0.1% to 111.32, sliding from a 20-year high of 111.81 hit early in the day following the conclusion
of the Fed's policy meeting on Wednesday. 
     The Fed issued new projections showing rates peaking at 4.6% next year with no cuts until 2024. It
raised its target interest rate range by another 75 basis points (bps) overnight to 3%-3.25%, as widely
expected. 
    The dollar was already supported by demand for safe-haven assets after Russian President Vladimir Putin
announced on Wednesday he would call up reservists to fight in Ukraine.
    Separately, the Swiss franc tumbled after Switzerland's central bank raised rates by 75 bps, when some
had talked up the possibility of a full percentage point move. 
    The dollar and euro both climbed roughly 1.2% against the franc, with the greenback last at 0.9783
francs and the euro at 0.9619 francs. 
    The Norwegian crown eased against the euro and dollar after the country's central bank hiked interest
rates by an expected 50 bps, and signalled a more gradual approach to tightening ahead. 
    The euro was last up 0.5% at 10.2203 crowns, while dollar rose 0.3% to 10.3955.

title: UPDATE 2-Norway  central bank  to buy more foreign  currency  for wealth fund
text:
(Adds Nordea comment, more background)

OSLO, Aug 31 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank said on Wednesday it would sharply increase its purchase of foreign currency for its sovereign wealth fund in September, amid a surge in the country's oil and gas revenues.

Norges Bank plans to exchange 3.5 billion Norwegian crowns ($355.41 million) per day into foreign currency, up from 1.5 billion per day in August, which will in turn be invested abroad by the $1.2 trillion wealth fund, already the world's largest.

DNB Markets had predicted in advance that Norges bank would increase the daily purchases to 2.5 billion Norwegian crowns.

The crown currency weakened on the news, falling to 9.90 against the euro at 0926 GMT from 9.82 just ahead of the announcement.

"This large shift points toward a weaker NOK ahead," said Nordea Markets, adding that the increase in currency purchase would also alleviate upward pressure on Norwegian interbank interest rates.

The crown may also in the time ahead be hit by stock market weakness, said Nordea, forecasting an exchange rate of 10.3 crowns per euro by year-end.

This year's spike in the price of petroleum, Norway's main export, has led to a big inflow of tax revenues that exceeded government spending.

Economists have said that a larger purchase of foreign exchange, and thus larger sales volumes of crowns, may weaken the Norwegian currency.

Norges Bank says its transactions are conducted for fiscal reasons on behalf of the state, and are not to be regarded as market intervention.

Norway is western Europe's largest oil and gas producer, with daily output of more than 4 million barrels of oil equivalent. ($1 = 9.8477 Norwegian crowns) (Reporting by Terje Solsvik, Editing by Stine Jacobsen and Gareth Jones)

title: Norway Currency Interventions  Unlikely For Now -- Market Talk
text:
1048 GMT - Norway's central bank is likely to shelve its interventions in the foreign exchange market as the krone recovers against the euro, Commerzbank says. "Unless there is a renewed wave of NOK selling, there is no need for interventions with EUR/NOK slowly drifting further downwards," Commerzbank FX analyst Antje Praefcke says. Oil prices and risk appetite will continue to drive the krone's moves in the short term, she says. EUR/NOK falls 0.4% to 10.9901.(renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1038 GMT - CreditSights is advising clients not to buy Telefonica 's 7.25-year and 12-year euro bonds on offer Wednesday at a spread lower than 32 basis points below their initial price talks. This means buying the 7.25-year bond at a spread up to 133 bps over the mid-swap level, which implies a yield of 1.08% and buying the 12-year bond at a spread of up to 173 bps over mid-swaps, implying a yield of 1.65%. These levels offer a new premium concession of 5 basis points over Telefonica 's comparable existing bonds, says the credit research firm. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

1023 GMT - The 11.3% decline in the eurozone's industrial production in March is massive, but it will be even worse for April, says Bert Colijn , eurozone senior economist at ING. "From there on, there will be significant recovery as the reopening of plants will surely increase production from the very low April bottom," Colijn says. The recovery will be gradual due to the slow easing of measures, supply chain disruptions amid an uneven reopening of the global economy, and demand at lower levels than before the coronavirus crisis, he says. "It seems likely that production levels of 2017 will be out of sight for a long time to come," Colijn says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1003 GMT - The U.S. Federal Reserve probably won't take interest rates into negative territory but speculation of such a move could build and send the dollar lower, MUFG Bank says. President Donald Trump 's call for negative rates and expectations for a rate cut in the futures markets mean a speech by Fed Chairman Jerome Powell later Wednesday "will be important," MUFG's Derek Halpenny says. "Anything less than a forthright rejection of negative rates could well fuel further speculation of negative rates being possible," he says. "A deeper negative yield implied in the futures market could well start to weigh more on the dollar and is a source of downside risk we previously had not considered." The dollar index is steady at 99.954. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0958 GMT - The effects of the corona epidemic that Nordea had expected in Sweden's March inflation numbers came in April instead. Inflation is currently a bit tricky to interpret, but there is little doubt that price pressures are very low, Nordea says. "We expect the Riksbank to leave the repo rate unchanged at zero, but the record low inflation highlight risks of a rate cut." (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

0956 GMT - While it still remains unlikely, negative U.S. interest rates would give gold a "massive boost," Carsten Fritsch at Commerzbank says. Negative real rates have been one of the main drivers of gold's recent strength and expectations that they will linger for some time have led many analysts to expect gold to rise further this year. Negative interest rates would further push down real rates and reduce the opportunity cost of holding gold. "So far, the Fed has ruled out any such step" to cut rates below zero, says Fritsch, and it would be very surprising if Powell were to express a different tone" when he speaks later today. Still, speculation continues with some fed fund futures pricing in the possibility, he notes. (william.horner@wsj.com)

0921 GMT - Almost one-third of people in the UK expect to face a pay cut or lose their job in the next two to four weeks, according to a survey conducted by UBS . The poll results, based on 1,000 responses, also shows that about half of them have no savings or have enough to last for less than three months. 42% of the respondents expect their financial situation to worsen in the next year, the medium-income group being the most pessimistic. (xavier.fontdegloria@wsj.com)

0912 GMT - While the Riksbank will look through the energy-driven plunge in Swedish headline inflation , the further fall in underlying price pressures will be harder to ignore, so it's increasingly a question of "when" rather than "if" the bank cuts again, says Capital Economics . With resource utilisation falling off a cliff, underlying inflation is set for a prolonged period below the Riksbank 's 2.0% target, it says. While minutes published earlier this week showed the governing council did not think a policy rate cut would be effective at the moment, they appear to be keeping their powder dry until the recovery phase gathers pace, Capital Eocnomics says. "Accordingly, we still expect the bank to cut its policy rate back into negative territory later in the year."(dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

0910 GMT - The pound's modest gains in reaction to better-than-forecast first-quarter U.K. economic growth data are likely to be brief, ActivTrades says. Sterling's respite is "unlikely to be long-lived" as March, when the lockdown started, registered a record 5.8% monthly decline in gross domestic product, suggesting the second quarter figures will be "considerably worse," ActivTrades analyst Ricardo Evangelista says. The U.K. economy contracted 2.0% in the first quarter, according to the official preliminary estimate Wednesday, although that was smaller than the consensus forecast of 2.5%, he says. GBP/USD rises 0.1% to 1.2270 and EUR/GBP falls 0.2% to 0.8834. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0909 GMT - The Japanese yen should continue to strengthen against the dollar as the U.S. currency declines on the Federal Reserve 's actions, Societe Generale FX strategist Kit Juckes says. "The yen continues to disappoint those who think it should do better in times of crisis, yet it is still out-performing the dollar even as the latter benefits from its dominant status," Juckes says. "That makes long yen attractive for anyone who think that it is only a matter of time before the U.S. makes a more concerted effort to weaken its currency." The Fed could face pressure from President Donald Trump to cut interest rates further to curb the dollar's strength, he says. USD/JPY falls 0.1% to 107.012. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0907 GMT - The U.K.'s first-quarter economic contraction of 2.0% compares favorably with many other countries but that doesn't mean it is better placed than others, HSBC says. "Recall that the U.K. did not enter full lockdown until March 23," HSBC economist Elizabeth Martins says. "Although clearly, activity will have started to tail off before then, this 2% fall for an entire quarter actually reflects only a single week of full lockdown." The numbers for the second quarter "will be much worse," Martins says. HSBC expects the economy to shrink by a quarterly 13% in the second quarter as the U.K. remains largely locked down six weeks into the period while other European economies start to reopen. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0849 GMT - A marked rise in U.K. unemployment is likely to limit the economy's recovery after the coronavirus lockdown eases, EY Item Club says after data showed gross domestic product fell 2.0% in the first quarter. "EY Item Club predicts that the economy is unlikely to return to its size of the fourth quarter of 2019 until the first quarter of 2023," EY economist Howard Archer says. The U.K. economic forecasting group now expects U.K. GDP to drop 7.5% in 2020, compared to its previous estimate for a 6.8% decline. It also downgrades its forecast for second quarter GDP to a 15% quarterly fall from a 13% decrease. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

title: Norway Foreign Exchange Interventions  Unlikely -- Market Talk
text:
1157 ET - Norway's central bank is unlikely to act on its recent threat to intervene in the foreign exchange market to limit the krone's decline in the face of weak oil prices, Commerzbank says. "I think Norges Bank will not do much more than keep an eye on the development of EUR/NOK as we are still a long way off the levels seen in mid-March," Commerzbank FX analyst Antje Praefcke says. "Moreover, there is a risk that it would have to stand up against the market and would gain very little while intervening on a falling oil price." A weaker currency also helps exporters who are "having a tough time" due to coronavirus. EUR/NOK falls 1.8% to 11.4454 as oil prices recover. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1107 ET - The Polish zloty has much further to fall against the euro due to the impact of coronavirus on the country's economy, Rabobank says. With Poland's consumer confidence and labor market suffering from restrictions to contain the spread of coronavirus, private consumption could "fall significantly" in the coming months with "negative consequences for the entire economy," Rabobank FX strategist Piotr Matys says. "The latest set of data supports our argument that EUR/PLN has not peaked yet and the current period of consolidation marked as a descending triangle will be followed by another leg higher towards the global financial crisis high at 4.9307 over the one to three month horizon." EUR/PLN is last flat at 4.5465. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1105 ET - European leveraged issuance ceased completely in March as efforts to contain the coronavirus pandemic shattered businesses and markets, says Moody's Investors Service . "March leveraged finance issuance ground to a virtual halt with no bonds issued and only one $45 million loan launched," says the credit rating firm, adding that the lack of issuance reflected a "dramatic reversal" from February's activity. A volume of $10 billion bonds and loans were issued that month after a historic peak of $44 billion in January, it adds.(lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

1056 ET - Bank of America expects the dollar to appreciate further in coming months, particularly against commodity sensitive currencies such as the Norwegian krone and Canadian dollar following the recent collapse in oil prices. "The chaotic turn in the oil markets indicates likely downward macro pressure that will do more damage in the commodity space, putting pressure on commodity currencies," BofA analysts say. The dollar should benefit from demand for safe haven assets as markets focus on the "massive economic fallout" from coronavirus, they say. BofA expects USD/NOK to rise to as high as 11.47 this year, up from 10.5470 currently, and USD/CAD to hit a high of 1.55 compared to 1.4018 at present. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1002 ET - The Swedish krona would weaken on a possible interest rate cut by the central bank at its April 28 policy meeting to shield the economy from coronavirus, Rabobank says. There is speculation that the Riksbank could return to negative rates after data sparked concerns that the economy could this year see the "worst recession since World War II," Rabobank 's Jane Foley says. "EUR/SEK has been on an upward trend since 2012 and for the most part this will have been welcomed by the Riksbank given soft inflation and the importance of its export sector," she says. "If rates are pushed back below zero, the risk of a further extension of the uptrend will increase." EUR/SEK falls 0.4% to 10.8871. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0827 ET - Treasurys are little changed as extremely poor European economic data is offset by an uptick in oil prices. Traders will be paying attention at 11am when the Treasury Department announces the size of next week's note auctions, as analysts continue to debate how the market will digest increased issuance to finance economic rescue packages. The 10-year yield was recently 0.625% vs. 0.618% Wednesday. (sam.goldfarb@wsj.com)

0820 ET - The Swedish economic sentiment indicator recorded by far the biggest drop ever in April to stand at a record low of 58.6. Consumer confidence plunged to 73.9 from 89.4 and confidence in manufacturing industry dropped too, but could have been worse, says Nordea . Confidence in the total business sector dropped to 53.1, the lowest reading ever. All in all, sentiment plunged like never before, Nordea says, adding that a massive drop was expected but it's still painful to see. "The survey indicates a huge drop in GDP and close to a two digit decline. The downturn in 2Q is important, but even more important is for how long the standstill will last."(dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

0818 ET - The European Central Bank will have to overcome the likelihood of a higher loss in order to be able to buy 'fallen angels', corporate bonds that have been downgraded to junk status, says BNP Paribas . "The one item that might pose an issue to the ECB is the high risk profile of BB fallen angels and the fact that, unlike repo operations, no haircut protects the Eurosystem from potential losses," says the bank. This might explain why the ECB didn't announce the inclusion of fallen angels as eligible bonds of its bond purchase programmes, though it will accept 'fallen angels' as collateral for banks to access ultra-cheap loans, it says.(lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

0816 ET - The eurozone composite purchasing managers index plunged to a new record low of just 13.5 in April, confirming that an unprecedented contraction in gross domestic product is occurring, says Simon Wells , chief European economist at HSBC. This sharp decline means a big downside risk to HSBC 's forecast of GDP falling 11% in the second quarter. "Whatever the magnitude of slump, what is more important is the shape of the recovery and how quickly activity bounces back," Wells says. HSBC expects April to be the trough in European PMIs. As lockdowns are eased in some countries and exit strategies are discussed, some firms should see rising output in May, he says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

0815 ET - Metzler revises its forecasts for the year-end levels of 10-year German Bund and the 10-year U.S. Treasury yields. The coronavirus "has led to a downright crash of global economic activity, to unprecedented measures by the major central banks and to massive market distortions," Metzler says. In view of the pandemic, the economic consequences and the question of how to finance the costs incurred, it has adjusted yield forecasts. Metzler now sees the year-end level of the 10-year German Bund yield at -0.60%, compared with its previous forecast of -0.80%, and it sees the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield at 0.5% at year-end, down from its previous forecast of 1.2%. The 10-year German Bund yield trades at -0.416%, while the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield trades at 0.624%, according to Tradeweb . (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0811 ET - Hungary's central bank is likely to keep interest rates on hold at its April 28 policy meeting after unexpectedly raising lending rates earlier this month to shore up the forint, TD Securities says. "We think further tightening remains purely a function of EUR/HUF performance," TD strategist Izidor Flajsman says. "The higher the pair, the greater the odds of new hikes of short-term rates." If EUR/HUF tops 365, a deposit rate rise "would not be too much of a surprise." The central bank on April 7 raised its overnight and one-week collateralized loan rates to 1.85% from 0.9% and launched bond-buying and lending programs. EUR/HUF rises 0.2% to 357.706, having earlier reached a two-week high of 358.5825, according to FactSet. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0807 ET - The European Central Bank 's decision to relax collateral rules for high-yield corporate debt increases the likelihood that this paper will become eligible for purchase under the central bank's bond purchase program, says BNP Paribas . "We now think there is a 2/3 probability that BB fallen angel bonds that respect the collateral rules will be included as eligible paper for both the Corporate Sector Purchase Program and the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme, possibly as early as next week's ECB meeting." The ECB said it would allow banks to maintain their access to the central bank's ultra-cheap liquidity during the current crisis by using bonds that have been downgraded to junk as collateral. This would effectively shield the financial system from a wave of credit rating downgrades.(lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

By Terje Solsvik and Colm Fulton

OSLO/STOCKHOLM, April 3 (Reuters) - The Swedish and Norwegian currencies are expected to gradually recover from recent weakness against the euro and dollar in the next 12 months following a turbulent start this year, a Reuters poll of foreign exchange strategists showed on Friday.

Both countries are experiencing unprecedented drops in business activity amid global shutdowns to combat the coronavirus pandemic, and Norway has taken a double hit as the price of oil, its biggest export, has crashed.

The Norwegian crown tumbled to all-time lows in mid-March before staging a partial comeback when the central bank threatened to intervene in the currency market for the first time in more than two decades.

The Swedish crown similarly hit 11-year lows against the euro and its weakest level in 18 years against the dollar in recent weeks, although it too has recovered some lost ground along with a partial rebound in stock markets.

By this time next year, the Swedish crown is predicted to rise to a level of 10.6250 to the euro from 10.9506 currently, the median forecast showed, albeit with forecasts ranging from 10.10 to 11.40 per euro.

Nordea Markets, which predicted some short-term weakness for the Swedish crown, said the longer term prospects were brighter.

"Looking to the second half of this year, if things will have improved and we are past the coronavirus, in such an environment, the Swedish crown should gain some strength," Nordea Chief Analyst Niels Christensen said.

With public debt at 43-year lows, the government launched a raft of measures, including subsidies for shorter working hours, tax rebates and loan guarantees, while the central bank has poured money into the financial system.

The Norwegian crown is meanwhile seen trading at 10.60 to the euro one year from now, up from 11.26 currently and a 20% rise from the all-time low of 13.1678 set March 19.

The price of North Sea Brent crude, although still down 60% year-to-date, has risen in recent days amid signs a price war between Russia and Saudi Arabia could come to an end.

"Less downside risk to the oil price is likely a key driver of the crown's strength," Nordea Markets said of the Norwegian currency.

While Norges Bank has declined to comment on any level it might seek to establish for the Norwegian crown, the most recent movement in the currency was likely also driven by central bank intervention, Morgan Stanley said in a note to clients.

Norway has launched business loans, tax deferment and fiscal spending worth at least 360 billion Norwegian crowns ($35 billion) to aid the economy, and the central bank slashed its benchmark interest rate to record lows.

Ultimately, the duration of coronavirus lockdowns and their impact on the global economy could be key also to the Nordic currencies.

"We can easily get a new wave of market unrest and if so, smaller currencies will suffer," Nordea's Christensen said.

title: Norwegian Krone Soars on First Signs of Market  Intervention  in Over 20 Years
text:
The Norwegian krone posted its biggest daily gain in over a decade, as analysts point to likely market intervention by Norway's central bank.

The krone rose 5% against the dollar and 4.6% against the euro on Tuesday. It traded at 11.09 kroner to $1, rising the most in a day since March 2009.

According to Magne Ostnor, an FX strategist at DNB Markets, the move was likely an indication that the central bank is now intervening.

Norges Bank said last week that it was considering purchases of Norwegian kroner due to the recent high levels of volatility in the currency markets.

This would be the first time the central bank has bought kroner since 1999. At that time, Norway had an exchange rate target to the euro and would buy and sell kroner to keep the value within a set band. Several central banks regularly trade their own currencies to maintain a certain valuation, including the Swiss National Bank and the People's Bank of China.

Norges Bank has historically shied away from moves to prop up its currency, despite frequent volatility as a result of oil price fluctuations. Norway is Western Europe's biggest energy exporter. The krone is currently the worst performing of all G10 currencies, having lost more than a fifth of its value against the dollar since the beginning of the year.

The currency has been hit by a combination of a 54% reduction in the price of benchmark Brent crude since the beginning of the year and investors' preference for holding U.S. dollars above all other currencies during market turbulence. The continuing global health crisis from the coronavirus, coupled with an oil price war, has prompted investors around the world to liquidate assets for dollars.

Norway's pension funds have been exacerbating the currency's plunge by rebalancing their FX hedges on their portfolios, selling krone and buying dollars and euros, according to Joachim Bernhardsen, a global macro analyst at Nordea. This action amid the global selloff has reduced liquidity in the market.

"If you look back to last week, the market was basically not working," Mr. Bernhardsen said. Bid-ask spreads in the foreign exchange market were as much as four times higher than in normal conditions. The central bank is likely stepping in to smooth out trading conditions and restore liquidity, he said.

However, "it is a very jumpy market and even smaller volumes are moving markets a lot," he said.

The U.S. Federal Reserve has also recently intervened in global foreign exchange and money markets with the goal of improving liquidity, opening swap lines with 15 other central banks and providing $1.5 trillion into short-term borrowing through the repurchase market.

--Caitlin Ostroff contributed to this article.

title: CORRECTED-WRAPUP 1-Dollar rampage spurs  FX interventions , speculation of big G7 move
text:
(Corrects March 19 version of the story to fix dollar gain in paragraph 4)

By Karin Strohecker and Sujata Rao

LONDON, March 19 (Reuters) - From Brazil to Norway, policymakers are leaping to defend currencies against the onslaught of the dollar which scaled three-year peaks on Thursday, raising speculation that a joint move by the world's biggest central banks may be in the offing.

Unlikely, most market-watchers say. But these are unusual times, and Norway's central bank earlier in the day threatened to intervene to lift the crown, a step it hasn't taken in more than 20 years.

The warning followed the crown's 30% plunge versus the dollar in less than three weeks, though oil's price collapse contributed.

But the dollar's brutal ascent -- up 5% this month against a basket of peers -- has sent almost every other currency reeling. Amid the crisis caused by worries about how badly the coronavirus pandemic will hit the world economy, investors and companies around the world have been scrambling to get their hands on the market's most liquid currency.

That forced highly unexpected moves such as a 15 basis-point rate rise from Denmark to support its crown while other countries such as Russia and Brazil engaged in direct dollar-buying. And South Africa said it did not rule out emergency interventions.

Despite these efforts, a global stampede for dollar funding meant currencies across the world sank to multi-year or record lows against the greenback. Some relief came after the U.S. Federal Reserve opened $450 billion in swap lines to several central banks but the pressure broadly remains.

"If there is one currency causing problems right now and aggravating the sell-off in global asset markets, it is the U.S. dollar," ING Bank told clients.

Could the answer lie in large-scale global intervention to tame the greenback?

Most top central banks, with the exception perhaps of Switzerland, are committed to letting markets determine exchange rates. Yet many welcomed Norway's shift; Danske Bank economist Frank Jullum urged it to buy crowns "by the bucketful".

One issue is that piecemeal central bank interventions are often doomed to fail as individual economies usually lack the firepower to influence currency markets for any length of time But shock-and-awe moves such as the coordinated Group of Seven moves to weaken the yen, seen after the 9/11 terror attacks or the 2011 Japan tsunami, have worked.

Alternatively the United States could act alone, some say, noting that dollar strength was highly unwelcome at a time when the U.S. economy is headed for recession. The last time the Fed went out on its own was in the early 1990s under George H.W. Bush to stem a soaring dollar.

"The U.S. has brought in almost all its instruments, the one that hasn't been done is intervention - the stronger the dollar gets the more likely the U.S. government will consider intervening," said Thomas Flury, head of FX strategies at UBS Global Wealth Management's Chief Investment Office.

"Typical during past crises, FX interventions helped calm not only FX markets but also equities and brought credit spreads down and that is something they will be keen to do." 

              
              
              
              
OUTSIZE DOLLAR
              


Dollar strength will dismay not only those in the Trump administration, but others around the world because when the dollar rises, it tends to 'tighten' conditions through channels such as higher import prices or by forcing interest rate hikes to shield currencies.

That in turn risks triggering a full-blown emerging markets crisis, the pattern seen many times in the 20th century.

Its power is down to the outsize role it plays in keeping the world's financial systems ticking over, accounting for 40% of global trade flows, 50% of cross-border lending and 65-85% of the world's risk-free assets, according to Goldman Sachs.

"Dollar strength is unwelcome for the U.S. as it tightens financial conditions but for the rest of world it tightens financial conditions even more because many countries are highly dollarised or they have dollar debt," said Claire Dissaux, head of global economics & strategy at Millennium Global Investments.

She doubts so far the pain from the dollar is big enough for Washington to ponder intervention -- alone or with G7 peers -- and says containing the raging selloff in equity markets will be the greater focus.

Plus there are the logistics of coordinating such a move with other central banks, many of which will not be keen to see their own currencies strengthening even as world growth nosedives.

Without "credible commitment from a group of central banks it won't work," said Dissaux who believes the best option is more swap lines of the sort the Fed announced on Thursday

But it is not just the dollar rise that is hurting, but also the brutal volatility. Implied volatility, or expected price swings for some of the world's biggest currencies have rocketed to multi-year highs -- one-month Norwegian crown vol is over 30%, triple end-February levels. The euro, pound and all emerging market currencies paint a similar picture.

"The vols are unbelievable. Intervention would quickly kick that lower," Flury of UBS Wealth said, calling it "the fear factor".

(Reporting by Karin Strohecker and Sujata Rao, additional reporting by Tommy Wilkes; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

title: UPDATE 4- Norway  crown rallies as  central bank  says it may  intervene
text:
* Crown has lost one third of its value this year

* Fell in wake of coronavirus, oil price crash

* Norway's central bank last intervened in Jan 1999

* Also pledges more cash for banks

* 'Buy by the bucketful', Danske Bank's chief economist says (Adds currency move, liquidity for banks)

By Terje Solsvik and Gwladys Fouche

OSLO, March 19 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank said on Thursday it is considering entering the market to buy its own crown currency, triggering a rebound in the crown, which had lost a third of its value this year, in a step it has not taken since early 1999.

Norges Bank will also pump more cash into the banking system, offering loans lasting for up to 12 months to help alleviate effects of the coronavirus pandemic and a slide in the price of crude oil, Norway's biggest export.

The crown rallied following the statements, erasing intra-day losses against the euro, although Norges Bank declined to say whether any currency intervention had taken place.

Danske Bank Chief Economist Frank Jullum urged Norges Bank to buy "by the bucketful".

The crown rose to 12.2870 against the euro at 1144 GMT from an all-time low of 13.1678 earlier in the day, Refinitiv data showed.

"Norges Bank is continuously considering whether there is a need to intervene in the market by purchasing Norwegian kroner," Norges Bank said.

Danske Bank's Jullum said on Twitter that the central bank should buy heavily and refrain from announcing the volume of its interventions.

"One advice: please don't say how much per day, per week, etc or how much altogether, or what is the target for the NOK. Just go into the market and buy crowns, quietly, and by the bucketful," he wrote.

Norges Bank last intervened in the crown in January 1999, when its official goal was to keep the currency in a narrow band against those of its trading partners.

In 2001, the central bank's mandate switched to an inflation target, and the currency has since traded freely, even during the volatile months of the 2008-2009 financial crisis.

"In 2009 the central bank said that intervening to strengthen the NOK was not a credible strategy over time. But they can intervene if they see big, short-term movements, for instance due to reduced liquidity in the market," tweeted Handelsbanken Chief Economist Kari Due-Andresen.

Norway has huge foreign currency reserves, including the world's largest sovereign fund - worth $880 billion as of Thursday - although its value has tumbled from $1.17 trillion on Feb. 13 as global stock markets plunged. title: Norway 's  central bank  says has firm policy against  currency intervention  -paper
text:
OSLO, Dec 18 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank has a firm policy against intervening in the currency market and has no position on where the crown currency should be, central bank Governor Oeystein Olsen told national daily DN, confirming the bank's stance.

The crown has been hit in recent months by the plunge in oil prices and suffered its biggest intraday drop in decades on Monday. It recovered by the end of the day, but is still nearly 10 percent weaker against the euro and 22 percent weaker against the dollar than at the start of the year.

"Norges Bank has a clear policy that the interest rate is our tool," Olsen was quotes by the paper on Thursday. "We have a board decision stating that we won't intervene to affect the crown's level."

A fifth of Norway's GDP is generated by its offshore energy sector and the 45 percent drop in crude prices since June dragged the import weighted crown, the bank's preferred measure, to an all-time-low on Monday.

"We had a meeting (on Monday) summing up events and got an assessment of the driving forces," Olsen said. "But we were nowhere near having a crisis meeting."

"In a situation where the oil price has fallen as sharply as now, it's obvious that the crown weakening works as a buffer that counters the negative effects on the economy," Olsen said.

The currency's weakness strengthens the competitiveness of Norwegian exporters outside the energy sector.    (Reporting by Terje Solsvik; Editing by Susan Fenton)

The inconclusive Italian vote has left markets in limbo and will likely continue to grab attention Wednesday while investors will also focus on U.S. budget talks. In the Nordics, eyes will be on Swedish and Norwegian macro data.

"The one thing that seems clear after the Italian election is that nothing is clear at all and uncertainty will linger on," Nordea Markets said in a note.

The vote, which concluded Monday, was Italy's most globally watched election in decades and euro-zone debt worries flared up again this week as the election failed to produce a clear winner. Market participants had been keen to see a leadership with the potential to push through tough reforms to reduce the country's debt burden.

"With no coalition getting a majority in both houses of parliament, ingovernability has won for now," Nordea Markets said, adding it sees a high probability of new elections within the next few months.

Capital Economics said the political deadlock in Italy looks set to prompt a renewed bout of market pressure which may eventually force Italy to request a support package from the euro zone.

In addition to Italy, investors will also be focused on the U.S., where Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke is set to present a monetary policy report to the U.S. House Financial Services Committee after his address yesterday to the U.S. Senate Banking Committee.

Capital Economics said the testimony Tuesday confirmed that the Federal Open Market Committee is paying a lot more attention to the potential costs of continuing with its quantitative easing this year.

"Bernanke still appears to believe that the benefits outweigh the costs, but the net benefits will continue to shrink as the Fed buys more assets this year," Capital Economics said, adding it is looking more likely the Federal Reserve will slow the pace of its monthly buys soon even if it doesn't see the desired improvement in labor market conditions.

Key for market participants this week is also Friday's deadline for U.S. policymakers to agree on spending cuts. Unless lawmakers act to avoid it, some $85 billion in automatic spending cuts are due to be applied on March 1. The scheduled cuts were originally set to take effect at the start of this year before being pushed back for two months.

In the Nordic region Wednesday, investors can look forward to Swedish trade data and Norwegian unemployment figures in the morning.

"The one thing that seems clear after the Italian election is that nothing is clear at all and uncertainty will linger on," Nordea Markets said in a note.

Market participants had been keen to see a leadership with the potential to push through tough reforms to reduce the country's debt burden.

Capital Economics said the political deadlock in Italy looks set to prompt a renewed bout of market pressure which may eventually force Italy to request a support package from the euro zone.

"Bernanke still appears to believe that the benefits outweigh the costs, but the net benefits will continue to shrink as the Fed buys more assets this year," Capital Economics said, adding it is looking more likely the Federal Reserve will slow the pace of its monthly buys soon even if it doesn't see the desired improvement in labor market conditions.

Key for market participants this week is also Friday's deadline for U.S. policymakers to agree on spending cuts. The scheduled cuts were originally set to take effect at the start of this year before being pushed back for two months.

Norway's government intervened to end an offshore workers' strike just minutes ahead of a threatened lockout at the country's oil production sites, the labour ministry said Tuesday. "The strike is over," ministry spokesman Jan Richard Kjelstrup said. Brent prices tumbled as a result.

Jan Hodneland, a negotiator for the Norwegian Oil Industry Association, or OLF, employers' group, said the government made a "responsible choice."

The Norwegian oil bosses had sought government action Monday in a pension dispute with hundreds of workers that culminated in the industry lockout threat in Western Europe's largest oil and gas producer.

Tuesday sees a slew of data releases in the Nordics including Swedish industrial production figures, as well as June inflation data from Norway and Denmark.

Apart from Nordic data releases, focus will remain on developments in the wider euro zone. A constitutional court in Germany is set to have a first hearing over the constitutionality of Europe's new bailout fund, the European Stability Mechanism, and fiscal pact.

Although the pacts were backed by both houses of the German parliament, they don't become law until German President Joachim Gauk has signed them. The president was asked by the German federal constitutional court in Karlsruhe to delay his signature so that the court would have time to prove the constitutionality of the pacts.

The ESM and European fiscal pact are considered key to fortifying the euro zone. However, political adversaries have filed legal challenges against the new laws before Germany's highest court. The ESM was expected to be launched later this month, pending ratification by national governments.

Swedish industrial production in May is seen decreasing 4.8% compared to the same month a year ago, as demand for Swedish exports fades amid a weakening euro zone economy. However, the May figure is seen 0.6% higher compared to April.

Nordea strategists said Monday they were surprised by the extent and speed of the SEK strengthening. The bank revised its EUR/SEK forecasts downwards, and now sees the cross trading at 8.70 in early October.

29 May 2012 11:50 EDT DJ  Norges Bank Governor: Won't Intervene To Control Krone Exchange Rate


 
   By Kjetil Malkenes Hovland 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

OSLO (Dow Jones)--Norway's central bank will not intervene in the currency markets to avoid a stronger krone in the event of Greece leaving the euro and any resulting economic turmoil in the euro zone, its Governor Oystein Olsen told Dow Jones Newswires Tuesday.

Speaking on the sidelines of a parliamentary hearing about financial markets and asked whether Norges Bank is ready to take action to avoid investors seeking refuge in the Norwegian krone, Olsen said the bank doesn't usually intervene in the currency market, and hinted it might not even be necessary.

"We did not intervene [after the crisis] in 2008 to 2009," he said. "We have a steady policy on currency. We don't intervene in the currency market to affect or control the krone exchange rate. So my comments stop there. It's also uncertain which way the krone would move if the turmoil increases in Europe."

Norges Bank has previously said the krone is not refuge of choice for investors if the financial markets turn bad.

"Often, when there is real turmoil in the markets, the krone is not very [interesting], investors go to the Swiss franc, gold and dollar," said Deputy Governor Jan Qvigstad after Norges Bank's previous rate meeting on May 10. "With less turmoil, Norway could be a safe haven, but when the situation is really bad" other options become more favorable, he said.

Swedbank First Securities analyst Bjorn-Roger Wilhelmsen supported this view and said the krone tended to weaken when upheaval increased in the financial markets. "I believe that the trade-weighted krone exchange rate will weaken if Greece leaves the euro. I don't think much will happen against the euro, because the euro will weaken significantly. The NOK will first and foremost weaken against the dollar," he said.

Earlier Tuesday, Oystein Olsen told a parliamentary hearing on financial markets and regulation that the situation would be very challenging if Greece leaves the euro, and that "strong forces" in Greece and the euro countries are trying to avoid it.

Olsen also said Norges Bank is prepared to help Norwegian banks in the confusion that could arise following a Greek euro exit.

"I think the uncertainty is huge, and we have to live with that," he said. "You shouldn't rule out that a Greek exit could lead to contagion in other countries, leading to more turmoil in the financial markets. If that happens, we will be on alert immediately, watching what occurs in the financial markets and the funding markets for Norwegian banks."

If needed, Norges Bank will provide liquidity as it did in 2008 to 2009, he said.

Olsen also told Norwegian MPs that the idea of joint euro-zone bonds would be an "enormous reform," and would require a lot of work to design a system to replace each country's bonds.

At 1411 GMT, EUR/NOK traded at 7.5247.

title: RPT-Norwegian crown allure intact despite rate cut
text:
(Repeats Wednesday story, text unchanged)

 * Norwegian crown slides after surprise rate cut

 * Impact seen limited, will not dent the crown's allure

 * Crown to stay strong vs euro, dollar

 * But further falls possible vs Swedish crown 

 By Jessica Mortimer and Nia Williams

 LONDON, March 14 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank has fired a warning shot at speculators who drove the Norwegian crown to a nine-year high against the euro, but the country's oil-fuelled growth and safe-haven status mean long-term investors are set to keep buying the currency.

 The Norges Bank cut interest rates by 25 basis points to 1.5 percent, confounding market expectations for no change, and said more currency strength could prompt further reductions. Its decision hit the crown, which could slip again as short-term traders who had bet on a rise cut their losses. 

 But investors who do not believe the Norges Bank will intervene to stem currency appreciation in the way the Swiss National Bank has done, given Norway's still healthy growth outlook, are seen snapping up the currency at cheaper levels. 

 Even if Norway did intervene for the first time since 1999, it would not have the credibility of the SNB, which has a long track record of determined currency management. 

 "They (the Norges Bank) have done their work for now ... But of course if the oil price stays high and risk appetite is increasing we might see investors eager to buy the Norwegian crown again," said Kyrre Aamdahl, senior economist at Den Norske Bank in Oslo.

 The euro surged nearly 2 percent to a one-month high of 7.5925 crowns, taking it well above a recent nine-year low of 7.3927 crowns. The crown lost 2 percent versus the dollar

and slid sharply against the Swedish crown. 

 SEB chief currency strategist Carl Hammer said the euro could rise further, towards 7.60-7.70 crowns, but the bank would look to sell the single currency on rallies above that level.

 Analysts said the crown was unlikely to return to its recent highs in the near term. 

 But Norway's strong economy and the currency's links to oil make it attractive to investors seeking alternatives to the crisis-hit euro, especially with oil prices high. 

 The central bank may struggle to stem further gains given many of the reasons behind the crown's appeal are due to developments abroad which are outside its control.

 STRONG MESSAGE

 The bank's decision came as a surprise due to Norway's strong economy and rapidly rising house prices. Analysts said lower rates risked causing a housing bubble, which may fuel speculation the bank will hold off from further rate cuts.

 However, despite the many reasons to buy the crown, analysts said speculators may be wary given the Norges Bank had sent a strong message that it was serious about crown strength, and still had room to cut rates further if it needed to.

 "People will be very careful about buying back the Norwegian crown ... The central bank stated clearly that they would not hesitate to cut again if the crown were to strengthen substantially once again," said Niels Christensen, currency strategist at Nordea.

 Other factors may also weigh on the crown in the coming months.

 Some analysts warned oil prices risk falling from their current high levels, while SEB's Hammer said Norway may make "substantial" purchases of foreign assets through its oil fund in the second half of this year, which would have a negative impact on the currency.

 CONTRAST WITH SWEDEN

 The Norwegian central bank's strong concerns about currency strength contrast with statements made by the Swedish Riksbank, which could prompt a further steep correction in the Norwegian crown versus the Swedish crown.

 Sweden's central bank governor Stefan Ingves said at a rate-setting meeting last month that he expected the Swedish krona to strengthen in the months ahead, minutes of their discussion showed. 

 The Norwegian crown slid as low as 1.1741 Swedish crowns, taking it well below Wednesday's high just below 1.19 and the high of 1.2040 crowns hit on March 8.

 Traders said buying the Norwegian crown against the Swedish crown had been a very popular trade among long-term investors and it could fall further.

 "The Norges Bank is incredibly unwilling to accept further Norwegian crown strength, while the Riksbank has projected euro/Swedish crown to reach 8.50 by year-end (versus 8.9 crowns currently)," SEB's Hammer said. 

 In the longer-term SEB expect the Norwegian crown to fall to 1.10 Swedish crowns or even below, he said.

By Gwladys Fouche

JEVNAKER, Norway, March 11 (Reuters) - Norway is likely to slash the ratio of oil revenue it uses in the 2013 budget, its finance minister said on Sunday, as prospects for the Norwegian economy outshine Europe's and the country's currency reaches multi-year highs against the euro.

Oil-rich Norway, largely sheltered from the global economic crisis, has a spending rule that recommends limiting oil-revenue spending in most years to 4 percent of the value of its $604-billion sovereign wealth fund.

"In 2013, if little happens ... we will use significantly less than 4 percent from the oil fund," Sigbjoern Johnsen told reporters ahead of government budget negotiations for next year.

"It is important that we hold back on the use of oil money because prospects for the Norwegian economy are good."

Cutting the ratio of oil money Norway spends does not necessarily mean it will spend less oil money in absolute terms, however, as the size of the fund may grow.

Johnsen said the precise figure would be given in October.

"What we can do from the Norwegian government side is to ... use significantly less than 4 percent of the oil money ... And it looks like we will do that in 2012 and 2013."

The relative strength of the Norwegian crown against the euro, which makes larges swathes of the country's industry less competitive than foreign manufacturers, was also a significant factor in the setting of next year's state budget, he added.

"We have seen a strengthening of the crown over a long time. It is an important consideration when we set the parameters for the budget in 2013."

Norway's safe-haven crown currency hit a nine-year high against the euro on Monday, helped by a strong economy, high oil prices and the low risk of central bank intervention.

Johnsen repeated the growth of Norway's mainland economy, which excludes activity from the energy and shipping sectors, would be somewhat lower than the 3.1 percent the government had anticipated, due to lower expected growth in the rest of Europe.

An updated estimate for growth will be given in the revised budget in May, he said.

title: Nordic crowns shine as refuge from euro crisis
text:
* Norwegian crown rises to 9-year high against euro

* Swedish crown also buoyed by sound finances

* Small bond markets limit chance of intervention, big gains

By Anirban Nag

LONDON, Feb 21 (Reuters) - Investors seeking shelter from the euro zone debt crisis have driven the Norwegian and Swedish crowns higher as other currencies once viewed as safe havens rapidly lose their appeal.

The strength of the two crowns, which are backed by top-notch credit ratings, solid public finances and current account surpluses, has so far drawn muted expressions of official discomfort unlike the Swiss and Japanese authorities' aggressive action to curb the franc and yen.

In fact, say analysts, the small size of the Scandinavian bond markets are a hurdle to further big gains in the Norwegian and Swedish crowns and indeed could see their strength drain away quickly, leaving little reason for intervention.

But for now the Norwegian crown trades near a nine-year high against the euro while the Swedish currency stands close to a 10-month peak struck in mid-January.

"For investors seeking safety from the debt crisis these countries are AAA-rated with low levels of indebtness and offer sound financial stability," said Carl Hammer, chief currency strategist, at SEB Merchant Banking, Stockholm.

"But because their debt markets are small, liquidity is an issue and many euro zone reserve managers do not look at them. So their currencies will not gain to the full extent."

Demand for the two crowns picked up after the Swiss National Bank put a cap on the Swiss franc's exchange rate against the euro last September and discouraged safe-haven inflows that had pushed the currency to record highs.

Some of those flows turned to British government bonds, helping sterling, but after rating agency Moody's said last week it might cut the UK's triple-A ratings, Scandinavian currencies were left as the main beneficiaries in the near term.

Norway and Sweden are small, open economies that rely on exports. So stronger currencies will hurt growth and could lead to deflation, which policymakers seek to avoid.

This was the threat Switzerland and Japan have fought in recent months by intervention which has caught speculators napping and left them nursing losses.

By contrast, the Norwegian and Swedish central banks have room to ease monetary policy to support growth rather than intervene, analysts say, and in any case there has been no sign of deflation.

Sweden's Riksbank is rarely seen in the currency market while Norway's central bank, Norges Bank, has not intervened in the market since 1999.

"In our view we are unlikely to see more than verbal interventions (from Norges Bank) - and consider the probability of those low as well - which will only have a short-term effect on the Norwegian currency," said Commerzbank analyst Antje Praefcke.

SOLID FUNDAMENTALS

Sound public finances in Norway and Sweden have meant little need to borrow and issue bonds, limiting opportunities for investors. Figures from the OECD think-tank showed Norway's outstanding central government debt at the end of 2010 was $111.5 billion while Sweden's was $171.6 billion. Both were dwarfed by the $2.1 trillion outstanding for the UK.

Similarly, the Norwegian crown accounted for just 1.3 percent of global foreign exchange turnover, while the Swedish crown made up around 2.2 percent. That compared with 85 percent for the U.S. dollar.

This limited liquidity means swings in the two crowns can be fast and furious, with investors vulnerable to huge losses as they struggle to close their positions.

Between the Nokkie and Stokkie, as they are known in currency markets, investors have shown a preference for the former partly because non-EU member Norway is a huge exporter of oil and because many are wary of Sweden's close trade and financial links to the euro zone.

Swedish exports account for around 50 percent of gross domestic product with the bulk heading to the euro zone. Norway, on the other hand, is a global oil and commodity exporter, so this week's rise in oil prices translates into more revenues.

"Right now the Norwegian crown has momentum on its side and if oil prices continue to rise, it could be headed higher," said Niels Christensen, FX strategist at Nordea, Copenhagen.

"Its gains against the Swedish crown are also helping as investors like Norway's solid fundamentals more, but if global stocks get hit, then it will come under pressure."

OSLO, March 27 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank said on Friday it had not changed its view towards currency intervention, one day after Governor Svein Gjedrem said the bank will consider intervening.

"Gjedrem did not say anything that we haven't said before. Norges Bank's view on currency intervention has absolutely not changed," central bank spokeswoman Siv Meisingseth told Reuters.

In a speech in London, Gjedrem said Norges Bank will consider intervening if the crown becomes "out of line", adding this was not necessary at present.

The crown swung after the comments, as investors struggled to understand if Gjedrem signalled a new, more hands-on currency policy after the crown's sharp appreciation in past months.

Meisingseth said in addition to changing interest rates, Norges Bank can buy or sell crowns in the market to influence the exchange rate, although "normally the bank will not use interventions".

"Exchange market intervention, irrespective of whether currency is bought or sold, is not an appropriate instrument for influencing the crown over a longer period," Norges Bank said on its Web site, detailing its array of monetary policy instruments.

"However, interventions may be appropriate if the crown deviates substantially from the level that the bank judges to be reasonable in relation to fundamentals, and if exchange rate developments weaken the prospect of achieving the inflation target."

It said "interventions may also be appropriate in response to pronounced short-term crown fluctuations when liquidity in the foreign exchange market falls to a very low level."

Norges Bank said it has not intervened in the foreign exchange market since January 1999.

The crown, which some analysts said may become the world's new "safe haven currency", fell this week after Norges Bank cut its main rate by half a point to 2 percent and said borrowing costs may continue to fall to 1 percent in 2009. (Reporting by Wojciech Moskwa; editing by Chris Pizzey)

LONDON, March 26 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank will only consider intervening on the Norwegian crown (NOK) if the currency becomes "out of line", governor Svein Gjedrem said on Thursday, adding that this is not necessary at present.

"Our stated policy is that we may intervene in the currency market for liquidity reasons. Another reason would be if the value of the currency was out of line with fundamentals in the economy and hindered our possibility to reach our inflation target," Gjedrem said at a London presentation of the Norges Bank's Monetary Policy Report after it cut interest rates by 50 basis points to 2.0 percent on Wednesday.

"When it comes to interventions in the currency markets, we have not done that since January 1999," he said, adding that those conditions for intervention had not so far been met.

The bank's mandate is to target core inflation of 2.5 percent in the medium term.

"We are a very small and open economy. The development in our currency influences price inflation and the real economy more strongly than in most countries. We have seen large swings in our currency," he said.

Gjedrem noted that the Norwegian crown weakened against the euro and the dollar until the end of the fourth quarter, then started appreciating against both. The crown has gained about 10 percent versus the euro this year after reaching all-time lows against the single European currency at the end of 2008.

"If we did (intervene), we would communicate it well in advance," he added.

Asked by Reuters whether he saw the crown as a safe haven currency, he said: "No. With oil prices changing so fast it cannot (be described as a safe haven currency)."

NO SPACE FOR BOND BUYBACKS, OIS MONEY MARKET

Gjedrem said the country's capital market was too small to afford a buyback of fixed income assets of the type carried out by central banks in the United Kingdom or the United States to kickstart stalling economies.

"We don't have the kind of market to buy as others do. It is not a very deep domestic currency (government) bond market, nor for commercial bonds, because most big companies borrow in foreign currencies as they are so export-orientated," he said.

Gjedrem also said there was insufficient liquidity in Norway, which is not a member of the European Union, to establish an OIS market as seen in other countries. He said there was not enough overnight market trading to achieve this.

The Overnight Index Swap rates are used as a base line for calculating a spread with three-month interbank offered rates in the money market which is an indicator of the propensity for banks to lend.

"The crown market depends on international money markets. When banks lend to each other its via the swaps market. The market is too small to establish that (OIS) sophisticated kind of market," he said.

OIL FUND NOT PROVINCE OF FINE-TUNING

The $323 billion Norwegian sovereign wealth fund, Europe's biggest shareholder, is in the process of shifting from a policy of investing 40 percent in equities to 60 percent, while reducing its fixed-income component to 40 percent.

Yet, last year, the fund lost 633 billion crowns, nearly $90 billion) on investments, posting its weakest return in the 10-year history of the fund, a negative 23.3 percent. [ID:nLB219293]

Gjedrem said it was not appropriate to "fine-tune" the fund by putting off a decision to invest more in equities.

"We don't try to fine-tune this. A decision was taken to increase the allocation to equities to 60 percent from 40 percent. We have a strategy largely based on indexing," he said.

"So we buy a lot when equity prices go down, and not so much when equity prices rise." (Reporting by George Matlock; Editing by Victoria Main)

title: Norway Fin Min Calls Krone Overvalued;No Action Signaled
text:
STOCKHOLM -(Dow Jones)- Norwegian Finance Minister Per-Kristian Foss repeated Thursday that he considers the krone to be overvalued. 

 "The message from the Minister is that we think the krone is being overestimated," said Kaj Martin Georgsen, political advisor to Foss. 

 The finance minister's comments were made at a seminar Aalesund, a town in northwestern Norway. 

 Specific action like market intervention or interest rate cuts wasn't touched upon by Foss Thursday, according to Georgsen. He added that the Minister has mentioned previously that the krone is overvalued. 

 A Norwegian-language news wire, NTB, and a Norwegian  Internet news site, Nettavisen, reported the remarks by Foss. Some participants in foreign-exchange markets misinterpreted the articles as the announcement of active measures to bring down the krone's strength. 

 The euro soared against the krone on the news, but when the finance minister's comments were put in the proper context, the single currency surrendered part of its gain. Neither of the Norwegian-language articles directly quoted Foss as saying he intended to break the krone's strength. 

 The euro had jumped above NOK7.2600 from record-low levels around NOK7.2200 as rumors of Norwegian government action to weaken the krone circulated in markets, but fell back when Foss' remarks were clarified. Early afternoon in New York, the euro fetched NOK7.2414 in thin trading. 

 Against the dollar Thursday, the krone reached its strongest point since April 1997, with the greenback sinking as far as NOK6.8505. In afternoon trading in New York, the dollar had recovered to NOK6.9050. 

 As investors worry about war with Iraq and higher oil prices, the krone has gained dramatically on both the euro and the dollar. With its vast deposits of offshore petroleum, Norway benefits when the price of oil rises. The country also boasts a hefty current account surplus and the highest interest rates in the western world, making the krone an attractive option for investors. 

 However, the strong krone hurts Norway's non-petroleum sector by making Norwegian manufactured exports more expensive in world markets. 

 Georgsen said the Ministry of Finance expects Norway's general economic policies to help to bring down the exchange rate sometime during the spring. 

 "The strength of the Norwegian krone seems to be too high when we look at the real economy of this country," said Georgsen. 

 -By Rod Stone, Dow Jones Newswires; +46 8 545 13094; rod.stone@dowjones. 

 (Robert Flint in New York contributed to this article.)

title: ANALYSIS-Robust Norway crown unlikely to vex  central bank .
text:
LONDON, April 9 (Reuters) - The Middle East conflict and higher oil prices sent the Norwegian crown to yet another record high against the euro on Tuesday but analysts doubted this would trigger any action from the central bank. 

 The oil-backed currency, which has been almost constantly hitting record peaks versus the euro since January, reached comparable levels in early 1997, prompting the central bank to intervene by selling more than 20 billion crowns and slashing rates twice in two days. 

 But this time round, economists expect the bank to keep its rates unchanged at 6.5 percent when it meets on Wednesday. Moreover, they think direct intervention is highly unlikely. 

Norway, which is the third largest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia and Russia, has rates that are double those in the eurozone and which carry a juicy premium of 475 basis points over U.S. fed funds. 

 "The central bank has been surprisingly hawkish about trends in inflation and they are concerned about the tight domestic labour market, which gives them some justification for why they are reluctant to cut rates," said Juli Collins-Thompson, senior economist at BNP Paribas. 

 "We had such a rally in the crown and this is actually beneficial for their inflation profile." 

 The petrocurrency hit a record high of 7.6151 against the euro , according to Reuters data, and stayed close to its six-month peak of 8.6394 versus the greenback set last week. It also stands at a 15-month high in trade weighted terms, illustrating the currency's broad-based appeal. 

 "I don't think the current valuation of the crown is historically so strong. I'd be surprised to see the central bank stepping in to reverse the trend given formidable flows," said Steven Pearson, head of currency strategy at Halifax. 

 "The crown could go a lot higher in the short term given the strong Norwegian economy and prospects that interest rate differentials could widen in favour of the crown. Norway is a lot closer to raising rates than the U.S. or the eurozone." 

 EVENLY BALANCED 

 The situation in the Middle East is also benefiting currencies that run large current account surpluses as any escalation in risk aversion highlights trade flows instead of capital flows as the main driver of currency movements. 

 Estimated in 2001 by the IMF at 12.5 percent of gross domestic product, Norway's current account surplus is among the biggest in the world. 

 The domestic economy enjoys one of the highest growth rates among developed countries with high revenues from oil helping to insulate Norway from the global downturn. 

 Last month, the bank shifted to a neutral outlook for rates from an easing bias, reflecting diminished worries the downturn would brake inflation in Norway to below the target. 

 The bank shifted last year to target inflation of 2.5 percent in two years' time, dropping a goal of crown stability against the euro. 

 Economists predict Norway's annual inflation rate to have remained at a six-year low of 0.8 percent in March. Such predictions underpin market forecasts for unchanged rates on Wednesday. The consumer price index is due also on Wednesday. 

 The labour market is indeed tight with official data showing the unemployment rate at 3.0 percent in March, far below that of the United States or the euro zone. 

 "Norway has almost full employment now and the central bank is concerned about wage growth and labour costs. But it's not in danger of missing its inflation target," Thompson said. 

 Analysts also believe that ongoing 2002 wage settlements, where workers are demanding higher wages and pension reform, could buoy wage growth, but the crown strength and the revised 2002 budget to be finalised in June could cushion inflationary pressure. 

 "Downward pressure on inflation from the crown strength is likely to be offset by the tight labour market and the risk of bigger-than-expected fiscal expansion, so we have a relatively balanced picture here," said Karl Johan Haarberg, senior analyst at Nordea in Oslo. 

 "I think the central bank learnt a lesson in 1997 that it can't fine-tune the market."

title: Norway  c.bank to give notice of any  intervention .
text:
OSLO, June 20 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank said on Wednesday that it would announce in advance if it plans to intervene in foreign exchange markets to prop up or depress the crown, but said the weapon would be used only rarely. 

 "Normally we wouldn't use it (intervention), but there could be special situations," central bank governor Svein Gjedrem told a news conference. 

 "If we were to intervene we would communicate it in advance. But we would not communicate the size" of intervention, he said. 

 Gjedrem was asked about the Norwegian central bank's intervention policy after Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, intervened in recent days to prop up the Swedish crown and stave off a growing inflationary threat. 

 He said any intervention would aim to reinforce the central bank's overriding goal of keeping inflation to 2.5 percent. Norway's crown, unlike the Swedish crown, was at record highs against the euro on Wednesday.

title: Norway c.bank to resume  forex  buying for oil fund.
text:
OSLO, March 25 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank said on Thursday it was resuming purchases of foreign currency for its Petroleum Fund, due to save cash for coming generations, and planned to buy between the equivalent of two to six billion crowns ($255 million-$770 million) in 1999. 

 "Norges Bank will resume market purchases of foreign currency for the accumulation of capital in the Government Petroleum Fund on March 25," it said in a statement. 

 "Daily purchases will amount to 20 million crowns in March," the central bank said. "In special cases Norges Bank may decide not to purchase foreign currency due to exchange rate developments." 

 The central bank suspended purchases of foreign currency last year for the Fund after a plunge in the price of oil, Norway's main export. It intervened heavily on the foreign exchange markets late last year in a bid to bolster the crown. 

 The central bank said it would publish daily purchase amounts in crowns for the following month on the last business day of each month at 10 a.m (0900 GMT). 

 "The amount may also be changed after the presentation of the National Budget and the Revised National Budget as a result of new estimates for annual transfers to the fund," it said. 

 The Petroleum Fund, set up for when oil and gas wells run dry next century, totalled 171.8 billion crowns at the end of 1998.

title: Norway foreign min plays down euro-crown link hope.
text:
OSLO, Jan 19 (Reuters) - Norwegian Foreign Minister Knut Vollebaek played down hopes on Tuesday of a currency intervention deal with the European Union to help bolster the crown, saying it would only make sense if the crown were pegged to the euro. 

 "Intervention accords only make economic sense within fixed rate regimes," he told parliament outlining Norway's policies towards Europe. "The Norwegian fixed rate regime was abandoned in 1992." 

 Prime Minister Kjell Magne Bondevik will visit European Commission President Jacques Santer on Tuesday in Brussels and German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder in Bonn on Wednesday for talks about non-member Norway's future relationship with the EU. 

 Norwegian opposition parties, which have a majority in parliament, have told Bondevik to investigate possible links between the euro and the crown, which has been weak in recent months due to a fall in the price of oil, Norway's main export. 

 Vollebaek reiterated that Norway, which voted "No" to EU membership in a 1994 referendum, had no plans to change its monetary policy to secure any deal on intervention with the European central bank. 

Norway's central bank hiked interest rates seven times in 1998 in a vain bid to keep the crown stable against European currencies before giving up in August and putting the currency into a virtual float. 

 Norway pegged the crown to the euro's forerunner, the European currency unit (Ecu) in 1990 until selling pressure forced the central bank to abandon the system in 1992. 

 Economists see little reason why the EU should offer Norway, led by a government opposed to membership, any concessions. Opposition parties have suggested Norway could get greater access to credit at the ECB to help possible intervention deals.

title: Europe Focus: No End To Krone's Woes In Sight Until Mid '99
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--The Norwegian krone looks set to fall back to its 1998 lows against the Deutsche mark, with little hope of a recovery until the middle of 1999 at the earliest, analysts said. 

 Weak commodity prices and the risk of an overheating of the domestic economy have battered the krone in recent weeks. Indeed, some analysts see the mark pushing up to its all-time high of NOK4.7180, reached in mid-October. 

Intervention by Norway's central bank, the Norges Bank, had helped the krone to stabilize into a NOK4.40-4.44 range. But with Brent crude oil futures trading at just under $10 a barrel - a 12 year-low - the krone's prospects look bleak. 

 "A more positive outlook for oil may have to wait for March 1999, when OPEC (Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries) oil ministers are next skeduled to meet," said Rebecca Patterson, currency analyst at J.P. Morgan Securities Ltd. 

 The global economic downturn and unusually warm early winter in North America are expected to keep a lid on demand for commodities prices in the first few months of the year. 

 "Should oil prices continue to weaken into early 1999 as we expect, price-supporting news of production cuts are more likely to emerge from the March meeting," Patterson said. 

 At 1456 GMT, the mark stood at NOK4.5425, down slightly from NOK4.5470 earlier but up from NOK4.5350 Wednesday.
