title: FX  IN EUROPE - Dollar soggy in flows-driven trade.
text:
LONDON, Dec 10 (Reuters) - The dollar fell to a one-month low against the mark in Europe on Thursday and was soft against the yen, undermined by sales from investors adjusting their holdings of the U.S. currency ahead of year-end. 

 Concern about a slowdown in U.S. growth have also prompted some selling, dealers said. The mark, meanwhile, has been underpinned by expectations that European interest rates will remain steady after last week's cut by the 11 nations due to start monetary union in January. 

 The dollar fell to a low of 1.6580 marks, its weakest since November 6, when it dropped to 1.6555, an area now eyed as near-term support. 

 "It's driven by flows. There are players unwinding dollar positions ahead of the end of the year," said Audrey Childe-Freeman, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy World Markets. 

 At 0825 GMT the dollar was at 1.6580/90 marks, down from 1.6690/6700 in late European trading on Wednesday. Against the yen it hovered just above a one-month low hit in Asian trading at 116.65, trading at 117.16/26, still down from 118.00/10 late on Wednesday. 

 Dealers said buying of Swiss francs featured in Europe, with dollar/Swiss hitting a one-month low below 1.35 Swiss francs and mark/Swiss at a five-week low of 81.30 centimes. 

 Even though dollar sentiment is bearish, there appeared to be little conviction to kick the dollar much lower through the bottom of its month-old range. 

 "The dollar's early push lower is indicative of the overall mood, but whether there is much follow-through is a moot point as volumes remain very thin," said Tim Fox, chief economist at Standard Chartered. 

 Dollar/yen recovered from its lows after Japanese Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa said his comment on Wednesday about forex levels did not refer to current market levels. He said Wednesday the U.S. was comfortable with levels at 110-120 yen. 

 Dealers said another negative backdrop for the dollar was the start of debate in the U.S. House of Representatives on Thursday about whether to remove President Bill Clinton from office for his conduct in the Monica Lewinsky affair. 

 In European currency trading, the mark surged against the Norwegian crown to a seven-week high just shy of 4.56 crowns. 

 Dealers said speculators felt encouraged to dump crowns amid expectations that Norway's central bank may have abandoned the use of intervention to support the crown after benchmark oil prices fell to 12-year lows below $10 earlier this week. Norway is the second biggest oil exporter after Saudi-Arabia. 

 Sterling came under pressure from the weaker dollar/mark but trading was sidelined ahead of an annoucement on interest rates by the Bank of England (BOE) at 1200 GMT. Britain is expected to cut interest rates by 25 or 50 basispoints in response to a flow of depressing economic data. 

 Significant moves in sterling would only happen if the BOE sprung a surprise by either keeping the repo rate steady at 6.75 percent of by an aggressive 75 basis points, dealers said. 

 The pound was at 2.7620/30 marks, down from 2.7665/75 marks late on Wednesday but off its low at 2.7578 marks. It was up against the weaker dollar at $1.6634/44, up from $1.6579/89.

title: FOCUS- Norway  c.bank says to resume  intervention .
text:
OSLO, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank, Norges Bank, said on Friday it was resuming interventions on the foreign exchange market to defend the crown, saying a recent plunge in the oil-backed currency was over-exaggerated. 

 The bank, which suspended monetary policy instruments in late August after seven successive interest rate hikes failed to halt a sharp depreciation in the crown, said the current slide in the currency was primarily due to international conditions. 

 "The Norwegian economic situation has not undergone substantial changes that justify such a weakening," the bank said in a statement. 

 The crown has declined sharply in recent days, falling overnight to new record lows against the mark mainly because of a renewed softening of oil prices, uncertainty over the 1999 budget and investors' aversion to minority currencies during unrest on international financial markets. 

 Following the bank's announcement, the currency recovered to 4.6775 against the mark at 0824 GMT after hitting a low at 4.7380 overnight. Against the inverse European currency unit index it was quoted at 114.29. 

 Norwegian monetary policy is orientated to return the crown over time to a range widely believed to be between 103 and 105 on the Ecu index. 

 The bank's attempts earlier this year to defend the currency led to a 4.50 percentage point surge in its key interest rates, sending the overnight lending rate to 10 percent and the discount rate to eight percent. Norway now has the highest interest rates in western Europe after Greece. 

 Norges Bank noted that monetary policy had resulted in a "significant widening of the interest rate differential" between the crown and European currencies. 

 "This interest rate level, combined with a tight fiscal policy, will also contribute to limiting inflation expectations," it said. "Against this background, Norges Bank will resume foreign exchange trading as part of its implementation of monetary policy." 

 In a speech in late August, central bank governor Kjell Storvik said that it was widely perceived that interventions, as a rule, had limited effect. 

 But Harald Boehn, head of the central bank's market operations, said on Friday that intervention had now become a more suitable tool. 

 "We have to a larger degree than previously been influenced by international factors which have affected the crown, and therefore interventions may be a more effective instrument," Boehn told Reuters. 

 Analysts said the bank's participation should help dampen excessive volatility in the currency. 

 "I think this will be stabilising and contribute to an appreciation of the crown," said Harald Magnus Andreassen, chief economist at Elcon securities. 

 "This is an extremely irrational market. This shows that Norges Bank doesn't believe it has earned such a weak crown and what that will mean for the dangers if increased inflation." 

 Others, however, said it might set off speculation. 

 "It's not obvious what will happen now. Norges Bank could stop the weakening trend we have seen, or this could start speculation all over again. Which of these will dominate it is too early to tell," said Solveig Erlandsen, economist at Handelsbanken.

text:
OSLO (Dow Jones)--Norway's central bank governor Kjell Storvik said Thursday that central bank intervention in the foreign exchange markets isn't a very effective tool to affect the value of currencies.

The survey of business executives at 460 service sector companies, covering about 40 percent of the German economic output had some cooling impact both on demand and business expectations.



At 1100 GMT mark/yen was trading at 78.38/40 compared with 78.68/70 in late Europe on Wednesday, while the mark was trading just off a nine-month high of 1.7297 per dollar.



Japanese Ministry of Finance official Haruhiko Kuroda said overnight the yen's correction from weakness has begun and that Japan was ready to intervene at any time.



His warnings were echoed by finance ministry colleague, Eisuke Sakakibara, who said it was risky to have large forex positions in the current conditions.



The mark also slipped back against the Swiss franc as safe-haven flows and the continued unwinding of carry trade supported the franc, pushing it to a seven-month high against the dollar.



"The market is generally unsettled about where it should be looking for safe-havens," said Steve Barrow, currency strategist at Bear Stearns in London. "But there is a lot of uncertainty and people don't have a clear idea of whether Swissie should become a super-strong currency or not."

title: FX  CROSS - Mark/yen falls through four-week lows.
text:
LONDON, Aug 20 (Reuters) - The mark fell to four-week lows against the yen and tested near-two-year highs against the Norwegian crown in European trade on Thursday. 

 As Japanese officials continued their battle against yen bears and markets continued to fret about the impact of Russian troubles on Germany, mark/yen continued to drift lower from the 5-1/2 year high at 82.80 seen last week. 

 "We've seen the mark hit by the fallout from Russia, too hard in my opinion. I think the economic impact is less than people think," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International. 

 Last week investors who were worried about Russia's economy and finances withdrew from the share and debt markets and concerns about the impact on German banks and exporters meant the mark also came under pressure, analysts said. 

 On Monday, Russia effectively devalued the rouble and announced a 90-day moratorium on some foreign debt payments. This development added to negative mark sentiment. 

 "And the yen has been talked higher by Japanese officials over the past eight days," Lyons said. 

 Japanese officials have warned of currency intervention in recent days. The latest was the head of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Bureau, Haruhiko Kuroda. 

 At 1304 GMT mark/yen was at 78.89/92, down from a Thursday high at 80.19 and versus 79.97/80.00 in late Europe on Wednesday. It has now fallen about five percent from last week's high. 

 A slowdown in Germany's July annualised M3 growth, which rose five percent from the fourth quarter of 1997 against 5.3 percent in June, dampened mark sentiment, as did a decision by the German central bank to leave interest rates on hold. 

 The Bundesbank, meeting for the first time after its four-week summer break, set the next two weekly securities repurchase tenders at an unchanged fixed rate of 3.30 percent. 

 Regarding the Norwegian crown, analysts said weak oil prices are behind the mark's rise to near-two-year-highs against Norway's currency. 

 Despite five interest rate hikes since March, the central Norges Bank has been unable to stem the decline in the crown. The last increment, on August 11, raised the deposit rate to 5.50 percent from five percent. 

 "The Norwegian crown is a classic example of a situation where higher interest rates don't help the currency," Lyons said. 

 Frequent intervention to support the crown by Norway's central bank has only tempered the crown's fall against the mark, traders said. 

 On Thursday, Norges Bank said it bought a net 426 million crowns between Wednesday and Friday last week. 

 The Norwegian crown was last at 4.2995/15 per mark after a session high at 4.3000 and versus 4.2940/60 per mark in late Wednesday trade. 

 The Norwegian crown's trade-weighted index was last at 105.82. Analysts said Norges Bank has in the past intervened or raised interest rates when this index has risen above 105. 

 The mark was fairly steady against the Swiss franc, it was last at 83.85/88 centimes vs 83.77/80 centimes late Wednesday.

title: Norway  NOK falls sharply, no sign of  intervention .
text:
OSLO, Aug 18 (Reuters) - The Norwegian crown weakened sharply on Tuesday with some players pointing to a steep rise in interest rates as driving the market. 

 Others said commodity-linked currencies were being hit across the board after Russia effectively devalued the rouble on Monday. It said on Tuesday that it would use all instruments possible, as well as precious metal reserves, to prop up the currency. 

 The crown fell to 4.2805 against the mark at 1300 GMT compared with 4.2705 at 1400 GMT on Tuesday. Against the inverse European currency unit index, it stood at 105.42 versus 105.17. 

 Despite the decline, dealers said there were no signs of the central bank stepping in to defend the currency. Norges Bank's mandate is to use monetary policy to maintain a stable crown against a basket of European currencies. 

 "Any country with a high dependency on commodity exports is being hammered today and Norway has one of the biggest exposures with oil accounting for something like 65 percent (of exports). Norway is very vulnerable," said a London-based dealer. 

 Other said the move was on the back of a run-up in short-term rates. Norway's three-month swap rate jumped 24 basis points on Tuesday to 6.20 percent and now stands 70 basis points above the official deposit rate at 5.50 percent. 

 The central bank announced a 0.50 percentage point rate hike on August 11 to support a depreciating crown and at the same time intervened on the foreign exchange market, buying 1.71 billion crowns between Monday and Tuesday last week. 

 The crown picked up slightly after the rate rise but has since slid back to levels below those seen before the last hike. 

 "The (central) bank is caught between a rock and a hard place. At the moment it is continuously following the market, which today has discounted another (rate) rise of 50 basis points," said a market player. 

 "It needs to go past market expectations, but at the same time is limited by what it can do, there is a risk they might be penalised for overkill." 

 Others said it was unclear what the central bank might do. 

 "The might want to wait and see if this is a spoof by the market or they might hammer it down fast. If they don't (intervene or raise rates), the market might take it as carte blanche to run the crown down," said Peter Warren, chief dealer at Finansbanken. 

 ((Tanya Pang, Oslo newsroom +47 22 42 50 41, fax +47 22 42 00 18, oslo.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Norway  C.Bank  intervenes  to buy crowns - traders.
text:
OSLO, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank, Norges Bank, intervened on the foreign exchange market on Tuesday to buy crowns to defend the flagging currency, traders said. 

 The crown continued to slide in early trade after oil prices tumbled almost 70 cents on the International Petroleum Exchange on Monday due to the glut in global supplies. 

 Dealers said a weak Swedish crown was also adding to the downward pressure on the Norwegian currency. 

 Norges Bank was not immediately available to comment on the intervention talk. 

 The crown stood at 4.2725 against the mark at 0944 GMT and at 105.29 versus the inverse European currency unit index. 

 It remained in a downtrend even though the central bank on Monday pushed up short-term money market rates by setting an interest rate of 5.40 percent for fixed-term deposits between August 11 and 13. It was the first time the bank has set a fixed rate since February. 

 The three-month swap rated continued to climb on Tuesday to stand at 5.91 percent at 0944 GMT compared with 5.77 percent at 1400 GMT on Monday. 

 Dealers said the oil price slide and weakness in the Swedish crown had outweighed the effect of the fixed deposit rate. "We would have gone firmer but reaction (to the fixed rate) became marginal because of the other factors," said a dealer. 

 The three-month swap rate historically stands around 40 basis points above the official discount rate, which is currently at 5.00 percent. The rate is now 90 basis points above the discount rate leaving room for a 0.50 percentage point rise in official rates. 

 Norges Bank last raised rates on July 6 to 5.00 percent for the discount rate and 7.00 percent for the overnight lending rate. It was the fourth rate hike this year to bolster the sliding crown. 

 At the same time the bank intervened to support the currency, the first time it had stepped into the foreign exchange market to defend the crown since January 1997. 

 Most recent figures from the bank on Monday showed it net bought 213 million crowns between Monday and Tuesday last week. The bank has historically been a net seller of crowns for the state's Petroleum Fund. 

 "Everyone believes in higher interest rates soon," said another dealer. "The intervention so far has been too small," he said. 

 ((Tanya Pang, Oslo newsroom +47 22 42 50 41, fax +47 22 42 00 18, oslo.newsroom@reuters.com)).

 "Interest rates are the most important means for stabilizing the krone," he said. 

 Storvik added that the central bank will not use large scale intervention to stabilize the krone. He admitted, however, that the central bank has been active in foreign exchange markets with moderate interventions in recent weeks. 

 In the month of July, Storvik said the central bank had intervened on the scale of 3.0 billion kroner to stabilize the krone. Storvik was talking at a press briefing after the central bank earlier in the day raised its interest rate corridor by 0.5 percentage point.

title: Nordic  Forex :  Norway  Krone Steady Late Amid  Intervention  Talk
text:
OSLO (Dow Jones)--Both the Norwegian and Swedish units are steady to slightly weaker against the Deutsche mark in late dealings Thursday compared to their quotes at the start of the day. 

 At 1429 GMT the mark fetched NOK4.2720, up slightly from NOK4.2670 in early dealings, and higher than NOK4.2640 at Wednesday's close. 

 But the Norwegian krone's relative steadiness has given rise to market speculation that Norges Bank, the country's central bank, has been in the market to bolster the currency. 

 "We haven't seen Norges Bank, but we have a suspicion that it might have been active in the market (buying kroner)," said a dealer with a Norwegian bank. 

 Although dealers conceded the krone may have been propped up a bit by some light commercial demand given its weakness, they still found it hard to believe the unit could hold up so well as it did amid negative pressures such as the weaker dollar and pound, low crude oil prices and a sagging domestic equities market, without any help. 

 Norges Bank's only monetary policy mandate is to keep the krone stable against other European currencies. So far this year it has boosted rates four times, and has periodically intervened to halt the currency's fall 

 "Sentiment for the krone is just negative," said the same dealer. He believed the Norwegian unit will hold in a range between NOK4.26 and NOK4.29 per mark in the medium term, with a bias for the weaker end of the scale. 

 But in order to stem the krone's slide, the trader argued Norges Bank would have to be decisive in its actions and raise interest rates instead of using small periodic interventions. 

 "Only a rate hike will do if the (selling) pressure mounts (on the krone," said an Oslo-based dealer. 

 Meanwhile, in neighboring Sweden the krona (SEK) moved lower against its German counterpart, and is quoted down to SEK4.5050, compared with SEK4.4885 at the start of the European day, amid a late but mild bout of selling interest.

title: Norges Bank Buys Kroner Vs Mark At About NOK4.25 - Dealers
text:
OSLO (Dow Jones)--Norges Bank, Norway's central bank, has intervened in the foreign exchange market Thursday, buying kroner against the Deutsche mark, dealers said. 

 Dealers said Norges Bank has been in the market several times buying kroner against the mark at the 4.2450 to NOK4.2500 levels. The volumes of Norges Bank's purchases weren't known. 

 "They (Norges Bank) are concentrating the buy orders on just a handful of institutions to keep it (the intervention) quiet," said a dealer with a Norwegian bank. 

 Norges Bank declined to comment. 

 The Norwegian krone has sagged in recent months because of an expansionary fiscal policy, a too generous wage settlement and plummeting crude oil prices. 

 That weakness has prompted the central bank to boost its key interest rate corridor four times this year, in order to stick to its only monetary policy of keeping the krone stable vis-a-vis European currencies. 

 (END) Dow Jones Newswires 09-07-98

title: Norway  C.Bank says  intervention  not suitable tool.
text:
OSLO, June 17 (Reuters) - Norway's central bank, Norges Bank, said on Wednesday intervention on a large scale on foreign exchange markets was not a suitable to maintain a stable exchange rate for the crown. 

 The bank said it would inform markets if it decided to intervene on any large scale again, a practice that it has not used since January 1997. 

 "Intervention on a large scale is not a suitable tool," Jan Qvigstad, a director at the central bank, told a news conference. 

 "Intervention can help flatten out (changes) in a single day when the market is thin," he said. 

 The crown, which has been depressed recently due to tumbling oil prices, government wrangling with opposition parties over the revised 1998 budget and high wage settlements, firmed slightly on Wednesday against the mark to 4.2345 compared with 4.2455 late on Tuesday.

title: Europe Focus: Norway Krone Gains Don't Kill Rate-Rise Fears
text:
OSLO (Dow Jones)--The Norwegian krone (NOK) gained some ground against the Deutsche mark Thursday, but the currency's advance wasn't enough to dispel market expectations of a central bank rate rise in the near term. 

 "The krone can't shake off the pressure that easily," said a dealer with one of Norway's biggest banks. 

 He said he expects the krone to be hurt by fears that spring wage negotiations among employers and unions will result in a generous wage settlement, which could drive up prices. He also noted concerns that the government's 1998 budget was too expansionary to cool down the booming economy. 

 Such concerns already have pushed the krone to around its lowest level since October 1996. And a weak krone boosts market expectations of an interest rate increase from Norges Bank, the Norwegian central bank, since the bank's only monetary policy mandate is to keep the krone stable versus European currencies. 

 In late trade Thursday the Deutsche mark fetched NOK4.2355, down from NOK4.2510 late in the previous session, and market sources noted that Norges Bank, the Central Bank of Norway, hadn't intervened to prop up the currency. 

 Peter Warren, chief dealer at Finansbanken in Oslo. attributed the krone's gains to a correction following a steep drop a day earlier, saying the mark had been overbought. 

 "There was krone buying from both domestic and foreign investors" Thursday, he said.

title: Norway has no plans to contact ECB on euro-Restad.
text:
OSLO, May 6 (Reuters) - Norwegian Finance Minister Gudmund Restad said on Wednesday Norway had no plan to contact the European Central Bank for possible cooperation on monetary policy after the launch of the euro from 1999. 

 "I don't think there is a special reason for contact. They know what we will do," Restad told a news conference. 

 Restad announced earlier that Norway would extend its policy of keeping the crown stable against foreign currencies after the euro supplants the Ecu from 1999. The Ecu is the current anchor of Norway's crown. 

 Restad also said there were no plans to seek a bilateral deal with the ECB on intervention to smooth out currency variations. 

Norway in 1990 pegged the crown to the Ecu and set up swap accords with European central banks in a strategy of joint intervention to smooth currency variations. 

 That deal collapsed in 1992 just before Norway abandoned the formal link with the Ecu.

title: Norway PM says monetary policy to stay unchanged.
text:
OSLO, Jan 21 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Kjell Magne Bondevik on Wednesday pledged to stick to Norway's monetary policy of a stable crown against European currencies and urged unions to limit wage demands for 1998. 

 "The existing flexible policy of a fixed rate will stay the same," Bondevik told a news conference. "The partners in the wage negotiations can rely on this." 

 The International Monetary Fund has suggested that Norway should shift monetary policy to a target of limiting inflation, away from the present overriding target of keeping the crown stable against the European currency unit. 

Norway says the existing policy, under which the central bank intervenes to smooth out swings in the exchange rate, helps unions and safeguards jobs by giving the big export sector greater predictability about future earnings. 

 Bondevik said that, with the "important premise" of a stable crown "we hope and believe that the wage round will succeed. We don't say without turbulence, there can be a good deal of that, but we hope that it will be agreed within an acceptable framework." 

 He said that workers had seen "considerable" hikes in real wages in recent years. 

 "The partners in working life are well served by moderate rises," he said. "Then it's easier to keep inflation and interest rates down and continue the fixed rate policy." 

 Officials say a switch to an inflation target could lead to higher interest rates to dampen growth in a booming oil-fuelled economy, and in turn spur demands for higher wages. 

 The IMF last month said the economy, bolstered by North Sea oil wealth, had begun to overheat and urged Norway either to hike short-term interest rates by about one percentage point or tighten fiscal policy. 

 ((Alister Doyle, Oslo newsroom +47 22 42 50 41, fax +47 22 42 00 18, oslo.newsroom@reuters.com))

title: Norway fin min says stable crown helps wage talks.
text:
OSLO, Dec 5 (Reuters) - Finance Minister Gudmund Restad on Friday reaffirmed Norway's monetary policy goal of keeping the crown stable on foreign exchange markets, saying it was an important tool to help keep a lid on wage rises. 

 "It is the government's target to stick to it (a stable crown). It is also an important condition among other things for wage negotiations," he told Reuters. 

 "If the condition of a stable crown is removed, I think it would be much harder to get agreement on a moderate wage round," he said. 

 He said that keeping wages in check at a time of strong economic growth by the oil-backed economy would be one of his biggest challenges in coming months. 

 Restad rejected suggestions by some economists that Norway should switch monetary policy to a goal of keeping inflation in check, away from the existing target of keeping the crown stable against a basket of European currencies. 

 He declined to say how big a swing was possible for the crown against a basket of European currencies under current guidelines. 

 Last month Norway's central bank, which intervenes regularly to keep the crown stable against the Ecu, urged greater flexibility in Norway's monetary policy, saying that it wanted to allow greater swings for the crown. 

 The Finance Ministry replied at the time that current guidelines allowed sufficient "flexibility". 

 Restad said that: "If there are situations with especially strong pressures on the crown in either direction, the crown rate can change in the short term, but the bank will use instruments so that the rate is brought back to the original range after a while."

title: Norway  C.Bank  intervened  to stabilise crown.
text:
OSLO, Oct 9 (Reuter) - Norway's central bank, Norges Bank, said on Thursday it been selling crowns on the foreign exchange market during the second half of September in order to stabilise the petrocurrency. 

 Norges Bank is often seen buying foreign currency as part of its role to manage the state's Petroleum Fund. 

 "We have intervened outside of the Petroleum Fund (acquisitons) since the second half of September," Leif Eide, a director at the bank, told Reuters. 

 The central bank said on Thursday it had sold 1.264 billion crowns between Wednesday and Friday last week. To date this year it has sold a net 55.932 billion crowns, it said. 

 As well as its role in managing the Petroleum Fund, Norges Bank also has the mandate from the government to use monetary policy to maintain a stable exchange rate of the crown against a basket of European currencies. 

 The Norwegian currency has appreciated strongly since mid-September, climbing around two percent against the inverse European Currency Unit (ECU) index and the mark, to which it touched around 3.98. 

 The crown has weakened slightly since last week and at 1300 GMT it stood at 99.22 versus the ECU index and at 4.0420 compared with the mark. 

 Eide said the intervention was due to the strength of the crown and short-term developments of the currency. 

 "The crown was not very stable and there were large swings during the day. Our intervention was to try and stabilise it," he said. 

 John Eriksen, analyst at I.D.E.A. in London, said the intervention confirmed that the central bank was uneasy about the crown's rapid appreciation, although this was not surprising given its goal of monetary policy. 

 "If the crown continues to strengthen we cannot rule out rate cuts despite the hot economy," Eriksen said. "But at the moment there doesn't seem to be a dramatic situation." 

 --Tanya Pang, Oslo newsroom +47 22 42 50 41

title: Nordic  Forex : Norway, Sweden Kr Sinks Vs DM On Foreign Sales
text:
OSLO (AP-Dow Jones)--Both the Norwegian and Swedish currencies are down against the Deutsche mark around midday Friday, compared with their levels earlier in the day, on foreign selling. 

 'We've been suffering from 'Scandi-mania' over past week,' said one trader said, citing heavy speculative buying of both the Norwegian and Swedish units from U.S. investment banks. 'However, foreign flows are now moving out, and it's a healthy correction.' the same trader added. 

 At 1145 GMT, the Deutsche mark was at 4.0770 Norwegian kroner, markedly up from 4.0625 kroner at the start of European trade, and even stronger than its quote 4.0465 kroner in Asian trade. 

 But volatility continues to be a dominant feature for the Norwegian unit, owing to Norway's indecisive parliamentary elections at the start of this week, traders said. 

 And if the Norwegian unit continues to exhibit big swings, traders argued the Norges Bank, Norway's central bank, may intervene to smooth the currency's fluctuations. 

 Meanwhile, the Swedish krona is also losing ground against the mark. 

 At 1145 GMT, the Deutsche mark fetched 4.2845 kroner, up from 4.2715 at the start of the day, but down a touch down from 4.2910 kronor late Thursday.

title: FOCUS-Norway crown firms on fixed deposit rate.
text:
OSLO, June 16 (Reuter) - The Norwegian crown bounced back from early lows on Thursday after Norway's central bank, Norges Bank, announced it had set an interest rate of 3.6 percent for its fixed-term deposit rate for the period July 1 to July 14. 

 Norges Bank regularly announces fixed-term deposits or fixed-term loans, which usually are carried out through ordinary auction, in order to control money market liquidity. 

 Analysts said the bank appeared to be testing the market's reaction to higher money market rates to see if it was enough to stabilise the crown. 

 "It is a clear signal that the central bank is uncomfortable with the situation of low interest rates and a weak crown and they want to put up money market rates," said an Oslo-based economist. 

 The crown pulled back to around the 4.1990 level against the mark immediately after the announcement from above 4.21. At 1200 GMT, it stood at 4.1970. 

 The bank has previously announced fixed interest rates at times of instability in the money market or if the fixed term collided with a repo arrangement, Leif Eide, department head at the bank said. 

 Eide said the bank's announcement was an attempt to carefully bring money market rates closer to the comparable ECU rates. 

 In the last auction between June 25 and July 1, the average fixed-term deposit rate was 3.46 percent and the highest rate was 3.52 percent. 

 At 1124 GMT, Norway's three-month money market rate stood at 3.59 percent, while the comparable ECU rate was 4.14 percent. 

 "Following the pressure against the crown half a year ago, we reduced official interest rates almost down to German levels," Eide told Reuters. 

 "Now the crown is more or less normalised, but interest rates are still considerably lower than ECU interest rates." 

 One London-based player said the move to a fixed rate could indicate a potential rise in official interest rates. 

 "This could be the first warning shot of a hike in official rates. The bank is concerned about the weak crown. It already has announced that it will begin intervention again to try and stabilise it. Now maybe they are giving an initial milder signal to the market. The potential threat is there," he said. 

 On June 17 Norges Bank lifted a self-imposed ban on intervention in the foreign exchange market in order to stabilise the currency. Norway uses monetary policy to stabilise the crown and the central bank intervenes to maintain a level that is not officially declared. 

 In January the bank announced it would stop intervening after three interest rate cuts in two months and extensive intervention failed to dampen a surge in the crown. 

Norway's official deposit rate is 3.25 percent and the overnight lending rate is 5.25 percent.

title: FOCUS-Norway  central bank  returns to  forex  market.
text:
OSLO, June 17 (Reuter) - Norway's central bank on Tuesday lifted a self-imposed ban on intervention in the foreign exchange market in order to stabilise the crown. 

 The bank said it had decided to reverse a decision in January not to step into the currrency market following a recent slide in the crown. Any intervention would be limited, however, it said. 

Norway uses monetary policy to stabilise the currency and the central bank intervenes to maintain a level that is not officially declared. 

 But on January 10 the bank, Norges Bank, announced it would stop intervening after three interest rate cuts in two months and extensive intervention failed to dampen a surge in the currency. 

 The bank, however, has continued to buy foreign currency in order to service Norway's huge Petroleum Fund, into which the budget surplus is pumped every year for investment abroad. 

 "Norges Bank's transactions in the foreign exchange market have since January 10 1997 been confined to regular purchases of foreign exchange for the equivalent of about NOK 3 billion per month for the Government Petroleum Fund," the central bank said in a statement. 

 "In the light of developments in the foreign exchange market, Norges Bank no longer finds it appropriate to maintain special limitations on the use of instruments for the purpose of exchange rate management," it said. 

 "This means we are lifting the self-imposed decision not to intervene," Leif Eide, executive director of monetary policy at the central bank, told Reuters. 

 "We don't see any strong pressure any more on the crown to appreciate," he added. 

 Recently the crown has weakened considerably, losing around two percent since June 3. 

 Market players attributed the fall to higher-than-expected inflation figures for May, weaker oil prices and growing concern over the outcome of parliamentary elections in September, based on recent opinion polls. 

 The thin Norwegian foreign exchange market means movements are often exaggerated in little volume. 

 The crown immediately rose on Tuesday as market players took the bank's announcement as a signal that the situation had normalised and that it wanted to stabilise the exchange rate. 

 At 0910 GMT it stood at 103.07 against the inverse European Currency Unit index and at 4.1930 against the mark, compared with 103.95 and 4.2310, respectively, at 0630 GMT. 

 Harald Andreassen, chief economist at Oslo-based Elcon Securities, said the bank's decision was sensible given recent strong fluctuations. 

 "It's better to use intervention than interest rates to stabilise short-term swings in the market. This is a very sensible solution," Andreassen said, adding that he saw little chance of the bank raising interest rates in the near future. 

 "In order for them to do that (raise interest rates) what they are doing today wouldn't work, but we already see that it is working," he said. 

 Stein Bruun, senior analyst at Orkla Finans, said the bank had sent a calming signal to both currency and money markets. But it was too early to tell if the crown's recent fall was a fundamental shift in the exchange level. 

 "The pace and the size of the weakening has been concerning but I think this was caused by a few sellers and a breaking of several technical levels. Foreigners are concerned about inflation and there's growing concern that the situation in parliament will be messy after the election. 

 "But on the other hand you have one of the best economies, there are not many countries with a budget surplus of six percent (of gross domestic product) and a current account of seven percent," Bruun said. 

 --Oslo newsroom, +47 22 42 50 41

title: Norway  c.bank lifts self-imposed  intervention  curb.
text:
OSLO, June 17 (Reuter) - Norway's central bank announced on Tuesday it no longer finds it necessary to maintain some self-imposed limits on its management of the crown exchange rate. 

 It said developments in the foreign exchange market, where the crown has weakened recently, facilitated such a move. 

 The bank on January 10 gave up trying to stop the crown from appreciating and said it would let the petrocurrency run its course for a while. 

 "Norges Bank's transactions in the foreign exchange market have since January 10, 1997 been confined to regular purchases of foreign exchange for the equivalent of about NOK 3 billion per month for the Government Petroleum Fund," the central bank said in a statement. 

 "In the light of developments in the foreign exchange market, Norges Bank no longer finds it appropriate to maintain special limitations on the use of instruments for the purpose of exchange rate management," it said. 

 "Any foreign exchange interventions will normally be undertaken with a view to curbing short-term fluctuations in the value of the Norwegian crown and will thus be on a limited scale," it said. 

 "This means we are lifting the self-imposed decision not to intervene," Leif Eide, executive director of monetary policy at the central bank, told Reuters. 

 "We don't see any strong pressure any more on the crown to appreciate," he added. 

 The crown stood at 4.2020 against the German mark at 0725 GMT, compared with 4.2125 against the mark at 1400 GMT on Monday.

title: Nordic  Forex : Norway's Krone Muscles Higher Against DM
text:
STOCKHOLM (AP-Dow Jones)--The remarkable rally in the Norwegian krone which forced the Norwegian central bank to cut its key rate twice in a week, continued Monday and late in the session the German mark had slipped close to 4.000 kronor. 

 At 1545 GMT the Deutsche mark changed hands at 4.0050 kroner, down from 4.0200 kronor in early morning trade, and markedly lower from 4.0370 kronor late Friday in Europe. 

 Traders accredited some of the strength to a generally weaker German mark but said that most of Monday's gains came in the wake of statements about interest rates and monetary policy over the weekend by Norway's finance minister, Jens Stoltenberg. 

 'The finance minister's comments added to last week's rally and the stronger it gets the more players seem to want to hop on the train,' said a trader at a major Scandinavian bank. 

 In an article in Oslo newspaper Aftenposten Stoltenberg said that 'there is room lower interest rates in Norway.' 

 Stoltenberg also said in Aftenposten that Norges Bank's decision Friday to step down its interventions in the foreign exchange market won't change Norway's main and only monetary policy goal of a stable currency. 

 The comments followed a busy week in the foreign exchange market, where Norges Bank cut key interest rates twice last week in an effort to stem the Norwegian krone's rapid appreciation. The central bank's key deposit rate now stands at 3.25% and the overnight lending at 5.25% 

 In the near term traders are taking a positive view on the krone but caution that the 4.000 kroner level presents a technical resistance level of some dignity. 

 'On top of that, in situations like this, not much is needed to provoke a wave of profit taking,' said one dealer.

title: Norway  bank cuts rates again, curbs  intervention .
text:
OSLO, Jan 10 (Reuter) - Norway's central bank, facing a runaway crown, cut official interest rates for the second time in two days on Friday only to see the oil-backed currency power to new peaks. 

 The beleaguered bank, buckling under market pressure, simultaneously announced it would now curb its massive but fruitless intervention and let the crown run its course for a while. 

 Effective immediately, the bank reduced the deposit rate and the overnight lending rate charged to commercial and savings banks by 25 basis points to 3.25 and 5.25 percent respectively. 

 But markets had discounted the cut, according to dealers. 

 Analysts say the crown is undervalued as the Norwegian economy is booming with huge surpluses in the national budget and current account. Norway is the world's second biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia. 

 Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg said the government had no plans to change currency policies despite failing to keep the strong crown from appreciating. 

 "We have not planned for that," Stoltenberg told reporters in response to a question. 

 He said the goal was to gradually return the crown to normal levels, but declined to say how this might be done. "I don't want to say anything about possible measures. The central bank has the operative responsibility. It is the job of a finance minister to be a bit unclear in some areas." 

 The bank on Wednesday announced a 50 basis point reduction in both rates effective Thursday, but in vain. Friday's cut also failed to slow down the crown's bull run. 

 "The crown exchange rate has recently been under persistent pressure," the bank said in a statement. "Norges Bank (central bank) has purchased foreign currency equivalent to 20 billion Norwegian crowns ($3.13 billion) since the start of 1997." 

 The primary objective of Norwegian monetary policy is exchange rate stability. The crown is in a dirty float, which means the central bank intervenes to maintain a level that is not officially declared. 

 Announcing a temporary policy shift, the bank said "...in the light of developments in the foreign exchange market, Norges Bank will not intervene to any substantial extent in the foreign exchange market over a period". 

 Oystein Stephansen at S-E Banken in Oslo, commenting on the bank's decision to curb intervention, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV): 

 "It means that the crown might be more volatile than we've seen before, that the markets are going to have a closer look at the crown, possibly test it towards the D-mark...We are going to see a new level for the crown. 

 "I expect it to stay there at least in the short term. We would have to see whether economic fundamentals then justify that level or whether we still have what you call an undervalued crown," Stephansen said. 

 The mark plunged to its lowest level against the Norwegian crown for more than four years because of a combination of weak German economic data released on Thursday and the curbing of intervention by the Norwegian central bank. 

 The mark/Norwegian crown rate fell to a low of 4.03 per mark before recovering to 4.0470/10 by midsession. At the start of this week the crown stood around 4.13 per mark.

title: FOCUS-Nordic  currency  gains to stay in spotlight.
text:
STOCKHOLM, Jan 10 (Reuter) - Nordic currencies, particularly the Norwegian crown, are expected to continue feeling upward pressure after lively central bank action on Friday ranging from market intervention to high-speed key rate cuts, dealers said. 

Norway's central bank, facing a runaway crown, cut official interest rates for the second time in two days on Friday only to see the currency power more than two percent in three days to a new four-year peak of 4.03 per mark at one stage. 

 Buckling under market pressure, the bank simultaneously announced it would now curb its massive but fruitless interventions and let the crown run its course for a while. 

 Dealers in Finland, Denmark and Sweden said their central banks had also sold their respective currencies, all of which have also been strengthening recently, for German marks. 

 The Norwegian and Swedish crowns have each risen more than two percent since January 7. The Danish crown and Finnish markka rises have been notable though less dramatic. 

 Dollar strength, coupled with strong economic growth prospects, have boosted currencies across the Nordic area although only Norway has so far seen the market test levels significant enough to force key rate cuts. 

 Oystein Stephansen at S-E Banken in Oslo told Reuters Financial Television the Norwegian central bank's decision to curb interventions would lead to more volatility. 

 "Markets are going to have a closer look at the crown, possibly test it towards the D-mark. It is a tough call today when the markets are moving very rapidly. We are going to see a new level for the crown," he said. 

 Sweden's Riksbank, eager to show the currency is stable without being linked to the European Union's Exchange Rate Mechansim (ERM), has already said it would enter the market to iron out sudden crown movements. 

 "It is a small stake to stop the strengthening of the crown in the international turbulence," one dealer said. "The Riksbank is not worried about the crown in itself." 

 Dealers said the dollar's recent surge has sparked interest in peripheral currencies, particularly in the Nordic ones because their economies have stronger than average European growth prospects. 

 Swedish economic think-tank KI forecasts gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 2.7 percent in 1997. Official forecasts for Finland are for GDP growth of up to four percent in 1997. 

 The Norwegian government said in its budget it expected 1997 GDP growth of 3.1 percent for the overall economy and 2.5 percent excluding oil production. For Denmark, consensus market forecasts are for 1997 GDP of 2.7 percent. 

 Analysts said these strong fundamentals suggest further gains for the Finnish markka, which has been linked to Europe's ERM since last October. 

 "On balance, there are strengthening pressures on the markka," SE-Banken's Helsinki chief economist Esko Torsti said.

title: FOCUS-Mark tumbles on Euro crosses, Norway shines.
text:
LONDON, Jan 10 (Reuter) - The mark weakened sharply on many of its European crosses on Friday, plunging to its lowest level against the Norwegian crown for more than four years and eroding key levels against the peseta. 

 The backdrop of weak German economic data released on Thursday helped to push the mark lower, while the apparent halting of intervention by the central banks of Norway and Spain sped up the decline, analysts said. 

 Many European countries have been locked in a struggle to prevent their currencies from appreciating further in order to avoid losing export competitiveness. 

 "As it is, the central banks of Norway and Spain appear to have given up the fight for the time being," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London. 

 But several other central banks were said to have jumped to the mark's defence in European morning trading as its weakness gathered momentum. 

 Dealers said the Bank of Finland sold markkas for marks, while the Bank of Portugal was seen buying marks for escudos. The Swedish Riksbank was also rumoured to have intervened in the market to slow the decline of the mark/Swedish crown rate. 

 The mark's slide accelerated after the Norwegian central bank said it would not intervene in the currency market for some time. It had been an aggressive seller of the crown recently to stem its appreciation, traders said. 

 The mark/Norwegian crown rate fell to a low of 4.03 per mark before recovering to 4.0470/10 by midsession. At the start of this week the crown stood around 4.13 per mark. 

 The crown is subject to a "dirty float", which means that the central bank intervenes to maintain a level that is not declared officially. 

 Announcing a temporary policy shift, the Norwegian bank said it would not intervene to any substantial extent in the foreign exchange market over a period. 

 The crown's surge forced the central bank to cut official interest rates for the second time this week, lowering the deposit and overnight rates by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.25 and 5.25 percent, respectively. 

 The Norwegian central bank said it had sold a cumulative 20 billion crowns ($3.1 billion) since the start of 1997. 

 Dealers said the mark/peseta rate fell through the key 84 peseta level as the Bank of Spain, which had been defending the mark heavily against the peseta since Wednesday, pulled its bids. 

 The Spanish central bank had been defending the 84 level for several months, they said. Its currency reserves have swollen considerably and rose by $1.64 billion in December to $61.83 billion. 

 The Norwegian crown has become a favourite for foreign exchange traders attracted by the solid fundamentals of the Norwegian economy, such as its huge, oil-related current account and fiscal surpluses, analysts said. 

 The recent rise in oil prices has been a boon for the crown as Norway is a key oil producer and exporter. 

 "There is a lot on the plus side for the Norwegian crown and a lot of investors are waking up to that," said Norfield. 

 The weak mark theme was reinforced by German data released on Thursday. 

 "It's not solely a Norwegian crown story," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London. "The weak German data helped revive speculation that German interest rates will be cut again." 

 German unemployment rose by 48,000 in December to 4.156 million, or 10.8 percent of the workforce. 

 Gross domestic product data reinforced perceptions that the German economy would remain in the doldrums for quite some time. 

 GDP rose by 1.4 percent last year after 1.9 percent growth in 1995. The economy stagnated in the final quarter with virtually no growth from the third quarter.

title: Norway Central Bank  says curbing  intervention .

title: Norway's NOK Weaker Against Most European Crosses
text:
OSLO (AP-DJ)--Norway's krone is slightly weaker against most European crosses, notably the Deutsche mark, in early-afternoon trade Monday. 

 In line with the pan-European trend, the krone is weakening against the mark as market players rally to the perceived safe haven of the German currency. In the spot market the mark traded at 4.3974 kroner at 1210 GMT Monday, up from 4.3875 kroner late afternoon Friday. 

 Measured on the unofficial ECU index, which moves inverse to the currency's strength, the krone is weaker at 103.74 points early afternoon Monday, from 103.66 points late afternoon Friday. 

 Last week, the krone strengthened against most other European crosses because of news that government revenues would increase dramatically on the back of higher-than-projected oil production. 

 Dealers say Norges Bank, the central bank, intervened late last week to weaken the krone. In Norway, the central bank frequently intervenes with small amounts to prevent the krone from strengthening or weakening too sharply, although the currency is officialy floating. 

 'I believe the krone will remain strong,' said a dealer with Finansbanken a.s. 'The fact that the krone strengthened substantially (last week) while the pound and the Swedish krona softened, is an indication of the market's long-term confidence in the currency.'

title: Norway's NOK Softer Against DEM, But Strong On ECU Index
text:
OSLO (AP-DJ)--Norway's krone is slipping against the Deutsche mark Friday, but is holding on to its strong gains against other European currencies as market players report the Norwegian central bank is selling off kroner in order to prevent the currency from firming further. 

 Although the Norwegian krone is officially floating, Norges Bank, Norway's central bank, regularly intervenes in the market with small amounts to keep the currency stable. 

 Against the Deutsche mark, the krone is weakening in line with most other European currencies. In early-afternoon trade Friday the mark is at 4.3908 kroner, up from 4.3865 kroner late afternoon Thursday. 

 But measured on the unofficial weighted ECU index, which moves inverse to the currency's strength, the krone is holding on to gains made earlier in the week. The krone is trading at 103.70 point on the index early afternoon Friday, little changed from late Thursday's level of 103.66 points. 

 Dealers say the krone firmed to 103.65 points on the ECU index Friday morning, its strongest level since the krone was allowed to float in 1992. 

 'But the central bank won't let the krone strengthen below the 103.70 level,' one dealer said. He said the bank is selling off kroner to offset a further strengthening of the krone against other European currencies. 

 'The central bank now has to make a decision whether its monetary policy should give priority to keeping inflation low or to increasing Norway's competitiveness,' said DnB Fonds, Norway's largest arbitrage company, in an analysis this week. 

 DnB Fonds said a tightening of monetary policies would strengthen the Norwegian krone. Such a policy would enable the bank to fight inflation, but would hurt Norwegian businesses' international competitiveness.

title: Norway's NOK Strengthens On Higher Oil Revenues
text:

title: Norway's NOK Firms; Trade Surplus Rose 54% Mo-On-Mo
text:
OSLO (AP-DJ)--Norway's krone is stronger against most European crosses Monday, notably against a broadly weaker British pound. Dealers said positive trade data released Monday supported the krone's strength. 

 At 1335 GMT the pound trades at 10.3995 kroner, down from 10.4090 kroner late Friday. 

 Measured on the unofficial ECU index, which moves inverse to the currency's strength, the krone is at 103.84 points in mid-afternoon trade Monday, compared with 103.90 points late Friday. 

 'The krone is now at its firmest level on the ECU index since November 1992,' said a dealer with Fokus Bank a.s. in Trondheim. 

 He said Norges Bank, the Norwegian central bank, regularly intervenes to weaken the krone when it strengthens beyond the 103.85 level on the ECU index. In Norway, the central bank frequently intervenes with small amounts, even though the currency is floating. 

 The dealer said there had been no sign of the central bank in the market so far Monday. 

 Against the Deutsche mark, however, the krone continues to weaken slightly Monday. At 1335 GMT the Deustche mark trades at 4.3796 kroner, up from 4.3753 late Friday. 

 Dealers said trade balance figures released Monday confirmed the krone's strong position. The data, released by the state statistics agency, showed that Norway's trade balance surplus rose 54% to 6.3 billion kroner in January, compared with 4.1 billion kroner a month earlier. 

 Compared with the year earlier, the trade surplus rose 33% from 4.7 billion kroner in January 1994. 

 Excluding the oil and offshore industry, there was a trade deficit in January of 3.6 billion kroner, the same as in January 1994, the statistics agency reported. 

 Meanwhile, in the money market, the Norwegian three-month interbank lending rate tightened to 5.63% Monday, from 5.47% Friday.

title: Norway Central Bank  Says 1994  Interventions  Balanced Out
text:
OSLO (AP-DJ)--Intervention in foreign exchange markets by Norges Bank, the central bank of Norway, balanced out last year and the net interventions 'amounted to virtually nothing,' Torstein Moland, the governor of Norges Bank said Thursday. 

 He said selling of foreign currency before the European Union membership referendum on Nov. 28 had been offset by buying of foreign currency when the krone began to firm after the referendum. 

 He said interest rates had fallen substantially since the referendum, but are still higher than a year ago. 

 The governor spoke to a group of economists gathered for a yearly currency seminar.

title: Norway's NOK Softens In Line With Other Scandinavian Units
text:
OSLO (AP-DJ)--The Norwegian krone is slightly weaker against most European crosses in very light trade mid-afternoon Wednesday. 

 Compared with last week, when the Scandinavian currencies suffered a broad softening streak because of turmoil on the international currency markets, the krone is firmer this week. But the Norwegain unit is trading within a wider range because of the thin volume. 

 'Last week, the krone moved within the range of 103.94 to 104.05 on the ECU index. Wednesday it has been moving between 103.83 and 104.00,' said a dealer with Handelsbanken in Oslo. The unofficial ECU index moves inversely to the currency's strength. 

 At 1400 GMT the krone is softer at 104.00 on the index, compared with 103.88 late afternoon Tuesday. 

 Although the krone is officially a floating currency, dealers say in practice the central bank, Norges Bank, will often smooth out ripples in the market with very limited interventions. 

 Dealers say the central bank tends to sell off small amounts of kroner when the currency dips below 104.00 on the ECU index. However, Norway's central bank reports its interventions only one week after the event. 

 'In line with the bank's policy, I can't comment on whether we have sold Norwegian kroner in the past few days,' said Leif Eide, director of market operations at Norway's central bank. 

 Against the Deutsche mark, the krone is softening in line with other Scandinavian currencies. The mark is trading at 4.3777 kroner at 1400 GMT, up from 4.3703 kroner late afternoon Tuesday. 

 In the money market, the Norwegian three-month interbank lending rate is unchanged from Tuesday at 5.74%.
